Rational symmetric functions from the Izergin–Korepin 19-vertex model
Alexandr Garbali Weiying Guo Michael Wheeler

Abstract




Abstract.

Starting from the Izergin–Korepin 19-vertex model in the quadrant, we introduce two families of rational multivariate functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
; these are in direct analogy with functions introduced by Borodin
[
Bor17
]
in the context of the higher-spin 6-vertex model in the quadrant.

(1)

We prove that
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
are symmetric functions in their alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
, and pair together to yield a Cauchy identity. Both properties are consequences of the Yang–Baxter equation of the model.

(2)

We show that, in an appropriate limit of the spectral parameters
\bm{z}
,
F_{S}
tends to a stable symmetric function denoted
H_{S}
. This leads to a simplified version of the Cauchy identity with a fully factorized kernel, and suggests self-duality of the functions
H_{S}
.

(3)

We obtain a symmetrization formula for the function
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, which exhibits its symmetry in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
. In contrast to the 6-vertex model, where
F^{6{\rm V}}_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is cast as a sum over the symmetric group
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
, the symmetrization formula in the 19-vertex model is over a larger set of objects that we define; we call these objects 2-permutations.

(4)

As a byproduct of the proof of our symmetrization formula, we obtain explicit formulas for the monodromy matrix elements of the 19-vertex model in a basis that renders them totally spatially symmetric.

Chapter 1
Introduction

1.1.
Background

The study of symmetric functions via integrable lattice models has become a very well established topic over the past two decades, elegantly blending techniques from algebraic combinatorics, mathematical physics, and representation theory. Perhaps the earliest incarnation of this correspondence may be traced back to the Jacobi–Trudi formula for Schur polynomials:

(1.1.1)

\displaystyle s_{\lambda}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})=\det\Big(h_{\lambda_{i}-i+j}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})\Big),

where
\lambda
is a partition and
h_{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
denotes the
k
-th complete symmetric function with finite alphabet
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})

[
Mac95
, Chapter I]
. As is well known,
h_{k}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
may be expressed as the partition function of a single monotone up-right path on the square lattice, such that the path takes a total of
k
horizontal and
N
vertical steps, and where a horizontal step receives a weight of
x_{i}
when it occurs in the
i
-th row of the lattice. By application of the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot Theorem, equation (
1.1.1
) then yields the famous non-intersecting lattice path formulation of the Schur polynomials; see, for example,
[
Ste90
]
. Such a construction strongly hints at connections with integrable vertex models, and indeed this turns out to be the case; numerous publications have explored partition function representations for the Schur polynomials, either in terms of the five-vertex model
[
ZJ09
,
BBF11
]
, or the phase model
[
Bog05
]
.

This connection extends more deeply into general symmetric polynomial theory. By now it is known that the Hall–Littlewood
[
Tsi06
,
WZJ16
]
,
q
–Whittaker
[
Kor13
,
BW21
]
, Lascoux–Leclerc–Thibon
[
CGKM22
,
ABW23
]
, Grothendieck
[
WZJ19
]
and Macdonald polynomials
[
CdGW15
,
GdGW17
,
GW20
]
may all be cast in terms of partition functions of appropriate vertex models. These representations usually provide elegant proofs of key properties of the symmetric functions in question, including their symmetry, branching rules, Cauchy identities and (in some cases) monomial positivity. The vertex models at play are various reductions of the six-vertex model — based on the quantized affine Lie algebra
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{1})
— and reductions of its higher rank analogues and/or higher dimensional representations.

A more novel direction, leading to deep connections with integrable probability, was discovered in the paper of Borodin
[
Bor17
]
. Rather than attempting to identify a given partition function with a known family in the general hierarchy, the approach of
[
Bor17
]
was to invent a new family of multivariate symmetric functions by studying the generic (higher-spin) six-vertex model in the quadrant. In contrast to the known families listed above, these new objects had the distinction of depending
rationally
on their underlying alphabet. Using little more than the Yang–Baxter integrability of the model, Borodin was able to prove several key properties of his rational functions, the most non-trivial of which being their Cauchy identities and orthogonality with respect to a certain deformation of the Macdonald scalar product
[
Mac95
, Chapter VI, Section 9]
. The work of
[
Bor17
]
, and those that immediately succeeded it
[
CP16
,
BP16
]
, led to a surge of developments in integrable probability, since the (stochastic) higher-spin six-vertex model degenerates to a host of known stochastic processes including the asymmetric simple exclusion process, zero-range processes, semi-directed polymers and the Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation. For a survey of these developments, and the extension of many of these ideas to the setting of higher-rank (or
coloured
) vertex models, we refer the reader to the introduction of
[
BW22
]
.

1.2.
Goal of present work

The aim of this paper is to extend the approach followed in
[
Bor17
]
to another known vertex model — based on the
twisted
quantized affine Lie algebra
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(2)}_{2})
— thereby defining a new family of rational symmetric multivariate functions, whose properties we study. This vertex model is usually called the
Izergin–Korepin nineteen-vertex model
or
IK model
for short.

The IK model, introduced in
[
IK81
]
, belongs to the general framework of solutions to the quantum Yang–Baxter equation
[
Jim86
,
Baz87
]
.
Since its introduction this model has been studied in the context of quantum spin chains
[
VR83
,
Tar88
,
WBN92
,
PLS14
,
Gar16
,
LCY+24
]
, loop models
[
Nie90a
,
Nie90b
,
FN15
,
GN17a
,
GN17b
,
MDP19
,
MDKP23
]
and in relation to discrete holomorphicity
[
dGLR13
,
IWWZJ13
]
.

In contrast with the six-vertex model, whose underlying state space is the set
\{0,1\}
, the state space in the IK model is three-dimensional; we denote its states by elements of the set
\{0,1,2\}
. In the integrable probability community it is standard to view the state assigned to a vertex edge as labelling the number of lattice
paths
which are collinear with that edge; accordingly, vertices in the IK model admit either 0, 1 or 2 paths per edge.

An important feature of the stochastic six-vertex model studied in the work
[
GS92
,
BCG16
,
Bor17
]
is its
sum-to-unity property
; this means that the row sums of the
R
-matrix of the model,
R(x;q)
, are all equal to 1. Combined with an appropriate positivity check for the vertex weights, this allows one to build a Markov process of randomly evolving paths in the quadrant; this process has several reductions to known stochastic systems
[
BP16
,
Agg17
]
. In the current work we find a non-standard gauge of the Izergin–Korepin model in which
R(x;q)
also has the sum-to-unity property, and use this exclusively throughout the text. Unfortunately, as is easily checked, there is no choice of the spectral parameter
x\in\mathbb{R}
and deformation parameter
q\in\mathbb{R}
that renders all entries of our
R
-matrix positive; this rules out any immediate probabilistic utility of the model.

Although probabilistic applications remain out of reach, we closely mimic the setup of
[
Bor17
]
and study the IK model in the quadrant, constructing two families of multivariate rational functions as partition functions with prescribed boundary conditions; we denote them
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
, where
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
are spectral parameters associated to the rows of the lattice,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
are spectral parameters associated to columns, and
S
denotes a 2-string (see Definition
1.5.1
, below). Using the Yang–Baxter equation and a handful of other intrinsic properties of the model, we prove the symmetry of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
in their first alphabets, Cauchy summation identities, and a symmetrization formula for the first family. For more details on our results, we refer the reader to Sections
1.4
–
1.9
.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to explore symmetric functions defined within a vertex model outside of the standard
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{n})
series
1
1

1

There should be no confusion here between the quantized affine Lie algebra that indexes the vertex model, and the root system underlying the symmetric function in question. For example, there have been some papers devoted to connections between symplectic characters/Koornwinder polynomials and vertex models; see
[
CGdGW16
,
FV17
]
. The former objects are based on the root system
(\widecheck{C}_{N},C_{N})
, and yet the vertex models used to study them were all members of the
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{n})
series.
.

1.3.
Disambiguation

The Yang–Baxter equation admits more than one nineteen-vertex solution
[
LS99
]
. The
Zamolodchikov–Fateev nineteen-vertex model
or
ZF model
is another example
[
ZF80
]
, and at the level of lattice configurations it is combinatorially identical to the IK model. The main point of difference is that the weights assigned to vertices in the ZF model can be obtained from the
fusion procedure

[
KRS81
]
applied to the six-vertex model (it corresponds to taking symmetric tensor representations of weight 2 of the underlying
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{1})
algebra, which lifts the two-dimensional modules of the six-vertex model to three-dimensional ones), whereas the weights assigned to vertices in the IK model cannot be recovered via fusion of any simpler model.

It follows that the IK rational symmetric functions studied in this work
cannot
be obtained via fusion of the functions studied in
[
Bor17
]
; but their direct analogues in the ZF model can be. Although we will not pursue this point further in the present work, we remark that the ZF model served as an important experimental tool for developing formulas with a nineteen-vertex flavour starting from known six-vertex ones.

Let us now give a more detailed overview of our results.

1.4.
Izergin–Korepin model with sum-to-unity property

The Izergin–Korepin
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(2)}_{2})
vertex model is an assignment of complex-valued weights to vertices:

(1.4.1)

Here
x
and
z
are variables associated to horizontal and vertical lines of the vertex, called
spectral parameters
; the vertex weight is a rational function in their ratio,
z/x
.
W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
also depends rationally on
q
, the
quantum deformation parameter
, but we shall suppress this dependence in most of our notations.

The model has a standard conservation property:
W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=0
unless
i+j=k+\ell
. Enforcing this constraint leads to nineteen possible non-zero vertex weights. In this work we present the model in a certain gauge that appears to be novel: our vertex weights satisfy the sum-to-unity property

(1.4.2)

\displaystyle\sum_{0\leqslant k,\ell\leqslant 2}W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=1,\qquad\forall\ i,j\in\{0,1,2\}.

Equation (
1.4.2
) would appear to pave the way to potential probabilistic applications; however, we were not able to find any choice of the parameters
x,z,q
such that all vertex weights
W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
are positive. Nevertheless, we chose to adopt vertex weight conventions such that (
1.4.2
) holds, since those weights have the greatest visual similarity with the conventions of
[
BW22
]
in the stochastic six-vertex setting. For the explicit definition of our vertex weights and the Yang–Baxter equation of the model, we refer the reader to Section
3.1
of the text.

1.5.
Symmetric functions

Before defining our families of rational functions, we introduce the notion of
n
-strings
, which are the combinatorial objects used to index them
2
2

2

In the higher-spin six-vertex model of
[
Bor17
]
, all symmetric functions are indexed by partitions. In that work, there is a natural bijection between states and partitions, in view of the fact that the top vertical lattice edges admit any non-negative integer number of paths, leading to a vector
(m_{0},m_{1},m_{2},\dots)
, where
m_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}\ \forall\ i\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
. That vector then provides a partition
\lambda=0^{m_{0}}1^{m_{1}}2^{m_{2}}\dots
written in multiplicative notation.
In the present text, all modules are finite dimensional (we take fundamental representations both in the six-vertex and nineteen-vertex cases). Reading the top vertical lattice edges leads to vectors of the form
(S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)
with
S_{i}\in\{0,1\}
in the six-vertex setting and
S_{i}\in\{0,1,2\}
in the nineteen-vertex model. At least in the latter case, there is no clear bijection with partitions, and accordingly we index all of our functions by strings.
:

Definition 1.5.1

(Definition
2.2.4
in text)
.

An
n
-string is an infinite vector
S=(S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)
with
0\leqslant S_{i}\leqslant n
for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
, and obeying the finiteness property
\exists\ M\in\mathbb{N}
such that
S_{i}=0
for all
i>M
. We write
|S|=\sum_{i\geqslant 1}S_{i}
for the sum of components of any
n
-string and refer to this quantity as its weight. Let
\mathfrak{s}(n)
denote the set of all
n
-strings.

Whenever
S_{i}=0
for all
i>M
, we make the identification
(S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)\equiv(S_{1},\dots,S_{M})
; we may do this without loss of generality, since the symmetric functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
that we define are invariant under the removal of tails of zeros from
S
.

Fix an integer
N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be an arbitrary 2-string such that
|S|=2N
. Our first family of rational functions is denoted
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
; here
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
denotes an arbitrary alphabet of cardinality
N
and
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
is a secondary infinite alphabet. We define them as partition functions constructed from the vertices (
1.4.1
):

(1.5.1)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}):=\hbox to260.1pt{\vbox to159.2pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 49.06618pt\lower-43.74947pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \color[rgb]{0.85,0.85,0.85}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.5pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}{}{}{}{{}}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 27.56 L 270.54 27.56}{fill:none} {{}{{}}{}{}{{}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{195.51846pt}{19.91684pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 270.54 27.56)} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 5.05 0 L -3.03 4.04 L 0 0 L -3.03 -4.04}{stroke:none} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {}{{}}{}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

In this picture, all bottom incoming and right outgoing edges are assigned the state 0. Every left incoming edge is assigned the state 2, while top outgoing edges correspond with the entries of
S
.

The object (
1.5.1
) is to be interpreted as a partition function in the statistical mechanical sense: one works out all possible labelling of internal lattice edges and assigns a weight to each such configuration, which is the product of all individual vertices that comprise it. Summing these weights across all possible configurations yields the rational function
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. See the left panel of Example
1.5.2
for a sample configuration of this partition function.

Introduce another integer
M\geqslant 1
and a new alphabet
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
; we take
S
and
\bm{z}
to be as previously. Our second family of rational functions is denoted
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
and defined as follows:

(1.5.2)

In this picture, all left incoming and right outgoing edges are assigned the state 0. The first

1.5.1
), the top outgoing edges correspond with the entries of
S
. We emphasize that in this definition, the number of horizontal rows,
M
, is independent of
N
. See the right panel of Example
1.5.2
for a sample configuration of this partition function.

Theorem 1.5.3

(Theorem
3.3.7
in text)
.

For any
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
,
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
are symmetric in their primary alphabets.

This theorem is an immediate consequence of the Yang–Baxter equation of the model and the particular choice of boundary conditions that we assign to left incoming and right outgoing edges; see Section
3.3.3
of the text.

1.6.
Cauchy identity

Having constructed our families of symmetric rational functions, we proceed to derive some of their properties. The first of these is their
Cauchy identity
:

Theorem 1.6.1

(Theorem
3.4.2
in text)
.

Fix alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
and an infinite alphabet
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
which satisfy the constraints (
3.4.1
), (
3.4.2
). We then have the summation identity

(1.6.1)

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}c_{S}(q)F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1})\\
=q^{N(2N+1)}F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})},

where the sum is taken over all 2-strings, the coefficient
c_{S}(q)
in the summand is given by (
3.4.4
), and where the function appearing on the right hand side is
F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
with
T=(2^{N},0,0,0,\dots)
.

Equation (
1.6.1
) is the first key result of this paper; its proof proceeds in several steps. We begin by noticing a certain
flip symmetry
of the function
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
that allows it to be written as a partition function similar to (
1.5.2
), but having undergone reflection about its central horizontal line and complementation of the states that live on horizontal lattice edges. This symmetry allows one to express the left hand side of (
1.6.1
) as a single partition function in the IK model; after permuting the rows of this partition function by
NM
applications of the Yang–Baxter equation, we arrive at the right hand side of (
1.6.1
).

1.7.
Stable symmetric functions

In the general classification of Cauchy summation identities, Theorem
1.6.1
is said to be of
skew
type, as the function
F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
resurfaces on its right hand side. Motivated by the quest for a Cauchy identity with a manifestly factorized right hand side, we were led to introduce a third family of symmetric rational functions in this work, which we denote
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. For their partition function definition, we refer the reader to Section
3.5
of the text.

These functions have several important properties which we believe render them more canonical than either of the families
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
. Their first property is that they are indexed by 2-strings
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
of
arbitrary even weight

|S|=2K\leqslant 2N
, and serve as generalizations of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. The latter are recovered when
S
is chosen to have maximal weight:

Proposition 1.7.1

(Remark
3.5.3
in text)
.

Let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a 2-string with
|S|=2N
. The following equality holds:

\displaystyle H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

Not only are the functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
special cases of
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, the converse also turns out to be true:

Theorem 1.7.2

(Theorem
3.5.4
in text)
.

Fix two integers
0\leqslant K<N
, and
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
such that
|S|=2K
. Let
\bm{u}\cup\bm{z}
denote the extended alphabet
(u_{1},\dots,u_{N-K})\cup(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
, and write
2^{N-K}\cup S=(2^{N-K},S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)
. The following reduction holds:

\displaystyle\lim_{u_{1}\rightarrow\infty}\cdots\lim_{u_{N-K}\rightarrow\infty}\Big\{F_{2^{N-K}\cup S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})\Big\}=H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

Their second key property is that they are
stable
with respect to their primary alphabet

(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
:

Proposition 1.7.3

(Proposition
3.5.7
in text)
.

For any 2-string
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
, we have

\displaystyle H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1},x_{N}=\infty;\bm{z})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\bm{z}),&\quad|S|\leqslant 2N-2,\\
\\
0,&\quad{\rm otherwise},\end{array}\right.

where the size of the primary alphabet on the right hand side of (
1.7.3
) is reduced to
N-1
.

The property (
1.7.3
) places the functions
H_{S}
on a similar footing to the stable spin Hall–Littlewood functions defined in
[
BW21
]
. Like the latter objects, the functions
H_{S}
pair together in their own Cauchy identity; this is their third key property:

Theorem 1.7.4

(Theorem
3.6.1
in text)
.

Fix alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
and an infinite alphabet
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
which satisfy the constraints (
3.4.1
), (
3.4.2
). We then have the summation identity

(1.7.4)

\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}(-1)^{|S|/2}q^{4MN-|S|^{2}}c_{S}(q)H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})H_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})},

where the sum is taken over all 2-strings and the coefficient
c_{S}(q)
in the summand is given by (
3.4.4
).

Equation (
1.7.4
) achieves our aim of writing a Cauchy summation identity with a factorized right hand side; its proof follows by taking a relatively routine limit of (
1.6.1
).

1.8.
Symmetrization identity

Although the partition function (
1.5.1
) provides an explicit construction of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, it is far from being a closed formula. Motivated by the goal of finding a
symmetrization identity
for the functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, we were led to the following definition and theorem.

Definition 1.8.1

(Definition
2.7.4
in text)
.

Fix two integers
n,N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(n)
be an
n
-string. An
n
-permutation matrix of size
N
and profile
S
is an
N\times\infty
matrix with all row sums equal to
n
, and
i
-th column sum equal to
S_{i}
for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
. We let
\mathfrak{M}_{n}(N,S)
denote the set of all such matrices
3
3

3

It is a potentially interesting problem to compute the cardinality of
\mathfrak{M}_{n}(N,S)
, although we will not report on this in the current text.
.

Remark 1.8.2
.

Note that
\mathfrak{M}_{1}(N,1^{N})
is just the standard
N
-dimensional representation of
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
.

Example 1.8.3
.

Let
n=N=2
and
S=(1,0,2,1)
, where we truncate
S
by deleting its infinite tail of zeros. The set
\mathfrak{M}_{2}(2,S)
consists of 4 matrices:

\displaystyle\mathfrak{M}_{2}(2,S)=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0&0&2&0\\
1&0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&1\\
0&0&2&0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1&0\\
0&0&1&1\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1&1\\
1&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}\right\}.

Theorem 1.8.4

(Theorem
3.8.9
in text)
.

Fix an integer
N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be any 2-string such that
|S|=2N
. We then have

(1.8.1)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{M}_{2}(N,S)}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\Delta_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)}(x_{i},x_{j};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}F_{\sigma(i)}(x_{i};\bm{z}),

where
\sigma(i)
denotes the
i
-th row of the 2-permutation matrix
\sigma
,
F_{\sigma(i)}(x_{i};\bm{z})
is a single-row (
N=1
) function (
1.5.1
), and

\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z}):\mathfrak{s}(2)\times\mathfrak{s}(2)\rightarrow\mathbb{Q}(x,y;\bm{z})
is an explicit rational function given by

\displaystyle\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z})=\begin{cases}\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\dfrac{(y-q^{2}x)(y-q^{3}x)}{(y-x)(y-qx)},&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&2&\\
\hline\cr V&&2&\end{tabular},\ \ \begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&2&&\\
\hline\cr V&&1&1\end{tabular},\ \ \begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&1&\\
\hline\cr V&&&2\end{tabular},\ \ \begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c|c}U&1&1&&\\
\hline\cr V&&&1&1\end{tabular}\\
\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\dfrac{(y-q^{2}x)(q^{2}y-x)}{(y-x)^{2}},&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&&1\\
\hline\cr V&&2&\end{tabular},\ \ \begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c|c}U&1&&&1\\
\hline\cr V&&1&1&\end{tabular}\\
\vskip 3.0pt plus 1.0pt minus 1.0pt\dfrac{(y-q^{2}x)^{2}(x-qy)}{(y-x)^{2}(y-qx)},&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c|c}U&1&&1&\\
\hline\cr V&&1&&1\end{tabular}\end{cases}

\displaystyle\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z})=\begin{cases}\dfrac{(q^{2}x-y)(xy+q^{2}xy-q^{3}yz_{k}-q^{3}xz_{k})}{q(1-q)(y-x)(y-qx)z_{k}},\quad&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&1&\\
\hline\cr V&1&&1\\
\hline\cr[1pt/1pt]&k&&\end{tabular}\\
\dfrac{(y-q^{2}x)(xy+q^{2}xy-q^{2}yz_{k}-q^{3}xz_{k})}{q(1-q)(y-x)^{2}z_{k}},&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&1&\\
\hline\cr V&&1&1\\
\hline\cr[1pt/1pt]&&k&\end{tabular}\\
\dfrac{(q^{2}x-y)(xy+q^{2}xy-q^{2}yz_{k}-q^{2}xz_{k})}{(1-q)(y-x)(y-qx)z_{k}},&\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&&1\\
\hline\cr V&&1&1\\
\hline\cr[1pt/1pt]&&&k\end{tabular}\end{cases}

\displaystyle\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z})=\frac{(xy+q^{2}xy-q^{3}yz_{k}-q^{3}xz_{k})(xy+q^{2}xy-q^{2}yz_{\ell}-q^{2}xz_{\ell})}{q(1-q)^{2}(y-qx)(x-qy)z_{k}z_{\ell}},\quad\quad\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c}U&1&1\\
\hline\cr V&1&1\\
\hline\cr[1pt/1pt]&k&$\ell$\end{tabular}

where any case of
\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z})
not listed above is determined by imposing the symmetry

(1.8.2)

\displaystyle\Delta_{U,V}(x,y;\bm{z})=\Delta_{V,U}(y,x;\bm{z}).

Here we have made use of the following shorthand, for any two rows
U=(U_{1},U_{2},\dots)
,
V=(V_{1},V_{2},\dots)
of
\sigma
and
a,b\in\{1,2\}
:

\displaystyle\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&a&&\\
\hline\cr V&&b&\end{tabular}\qquad\text{ indicates that }a\text{ in }U\text{ occurs before }b\text{ in }V,

\displaystyle\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&&a&\\
\hline\cr V&b&&\end{tabular}\qquad\text{ indicates that }a\text{ in }U\text{ occurs after }b\text{ in }V,

\displaystyle\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&a&&\\
\hline\cr V&b&&\end{tabular}\qquad\text{ indicates that }a\text{ in }U\text{ occurs at the same position as }b\text{ in }V,

\displaystyle\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&a&&\\
\hline\cr V&&b&\\
\hline\cr[1pt/1pt]&k&$\ell$&\end{tabular}\qquad\text{ indicates that }U_{k}=a\text{ and }V_{\ell}=b,\text{ with }1\leqslant k<\ell.

Remark 1.8.5
.

In view of the symmetry property (
1.8.2
) of the bivariate factors appearing in (
1.8.1
), it is easy to see that
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is invariant under the pairwise swaps
x_{i}\leftrightarrow x_{j}
. Hence, (
1.8.1
) manifestly exhibits the symmetry of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
in its first alphabet.

Equation (
1.8.1
) may appear somewhat unusual compared with traditional symmetrization identities, however it is quite easy to cast the corresponding result for the six-vertex model in a completely analogous way:

Theorem 1.8.6

(Theorem
2.7.5
in text)
.

Fix an integer
N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be any 1-string such that
|S|=N
. There holds

(1.8.3)

\displaystyle F^{6{\rm V}}_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{M}_{1}(N,S)}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\Delta^{6{\rm V}}_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)}(x_{i},x_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{N}F^{6{\rm V}}_{\sigma(i)}(x_{i};\bm{z}),

where
\sigma(i)
denotes the
i
-th row of the 1-permutation matrix
\sigma
, and where we have defined

\displaystyle\Delta^{6{\rm V}}_{U,V}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\dfrac{y-qx}{y-x},&\qquad\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&1&\\
\hline\cr V&&1&\end{tabular}\quad\text{(1 in $U$ occurs before 1 in $V$)},\\
\\
\dfrac{x-qy}{x-y},&\qquad\begin{tabular}[]{c||c|c|c}U&&1\\
\hline\cr V&1&&\end{tabular}\quad\text{(1 in $U$ occurs after 1 in $V$)},\end{array}\right.

for any
(U,V)\in\mathfrak{s}(1)\times\mathfrak{s}(1)
such that
|U|=|V|=1
.

Equation (
1.8.1
) is the second key result of this paper; it was also by far the most difficult to formulate and prove. The main challenge in generalizing the six-vertex result (
1.8.3
) to the IK case is that it is not
a priori
clear over what set of objects one should symmetrize, such that summands remain factorized. We initially arrived at a similar formula to (
1.8.1
) in the ZF model, by performing an appropriate fusion of the six-vertex formula (
1.8.3
). From there, aided by computer experiments, we were able to conjecture (
1.8.1
) in the IK setting. Even with an explicit conjecture in clear view, the proof of (
1.8.1
) remained a formidable challenge, since many of the techniques that expedite the proof of the six-vertex result (
1.8.3
) break down at the level of the IK model. The main challenge that one faces is that standard Lagrange interpolation techniques are more involved, since partition functions in the IK model (when viewed as polynomials in their spectral parameters) have double the degree of their six-vertex counterparts; as such, one requires twice the number of interpolating points.

Eventually we were able to find a set of Lagrange interpolation based properties for the functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, that uniquely characterize them. In order to show that the formula (
1.8.1
) satisfies these properties, it was necessary to find a subtle algebraic reformulation of it in terms of a family of operators called
twisted columns
, as we describe in the next subsection.

1.9.
Twisted columns

Our key algebraic tool in the proof of Theorem
1.8.4
is the introduction of a family of three operators
\Gamma_{0}(z),\Gamma_{1}(z),\Gamma_{2}(z)\in{\rm End}(V_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{N})
which live in an
N
-fold tensor product of the three-dimensional space
V\cong\mathbb{C}^{3}
. These operators depend implicitly on the full alphabet
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and the parameter
q
, as well as a single variable
z
; for notational compactness we shall only show dependence on the latter.

The simplest of these operators is
\Gamma_{0}(z)
:

\displaystyle\Gamma_{0}(z)=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\
0&\dfrac{1-z/x_{i}}{1-q^{2}z/x_{i}}&0\\
0&0&\dfrac{(1-z/x_{i})(1-qz/x_{i})}{(1-q^{2}z/x_{i})(1-q^{3}z/x_{i})}\end{pmatrix}_{i}\in{\rm End}(V_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{N}).

The remaining operators
\Gamma_{1}(z)
and
\Gamma_{2}(z)
are more complicated, but nevertheless fully explicit; see Section
3.8.2
of the text. Our main result concerning these operators is the following:

Theorem 1.9.1

(Proposition
3.8.2
and Theorem
3.8.3
in text)
.

For any
k\in\{0,1,2\}
and
1\leqslant i,j\leqslant N
, the operator
\Gamma_{k}(z)
is invariant under simultaneous permutation of the spaces
V_{i}\otimes V_{j}
in which it acts and the variables
(x_{i},x_{j})
upon which it depends. Further,
\langle\Gamma_{0}(z),\Gamma_{1}(z),\Gamma_{2}(z)\rangle
forms a subalgebra of the Yang–Baxter algebra for the Izergin–Korepin model.

The above result states the operators
\Gamma_{0}(z),\Gamma_{1}(z),\Gamma_{2}(z)
satisfy the same exchange relations as the column-to-column operators used to build the partition function (
1.5.1
), and are totally spatially symmetric (unlike the original operators). It is therefore reasonable to expect that
\Gamma_{0}(z),\Gamma_{1}(z),\Gamma_{2}(z)
constitute
Drinfeld twists
of our starting column-to-column operators; this is a highly non-trivial result, since to the best of our knowledge very little is known about factorizing twists in the
U_{q}(A^{(2)}_{2})
setting.

Using Theorem
1.9.1
, combined with the verification of appropriate (Lagrange interpolation) properties, we are finally able to show that

(1.9.1)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\mathopen{\hbox{${\langle}$}\kern-1.94444pt\hbox{${\langle}$}}2^{N}\|\Gamma_{S_{1}}(z_{1})\Gamma_{S_{2}}(z_{2})\Gamma_{S_{3}}(z_{3})\cdots\|0^{N}\mathclose{\hbox{${\rangle}$}\kern-1.94444pt\hbox{${\rangle}$}},

where
\|0^{N}\mathclose{\hbox{${\rangle}$}\kern-1.94444pt\hbox{${\rangle}$}}\in V_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{N}
and
\mathopen{\hbox{${\langle}$}\kern-1.94444pt\hbox{${\langle}$}}2^{N}\|\in V_{1}^{*}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{N}^{*}
denote highest (and lowest) weight vectors in the space in which the operators act (and its dual). This allows us to complete the proof of Theorem
1.8.4
, since the right hand side of (
1.9.1
) may be readily expanded to yield the right hand side of (
1.8.1
).

1.10.
Future directions

The work performed in this paper suggests a number of potential continuations; we elaborate briefly on some of these below.

•

Orthogonality.
One of the most important properties of the rational symmetric functions constructed in
[
Bor17
]
is their orthogonality with respect to a certain integral inner product; this result may in fact be traced back to the even earlier work
[
BCPS15a
,
BCPS15b
]
. The orthogonality relations of the functions, together with their Cauchy identity, allow for the construction of a generalized Fourier theory (complete with a forwards and backwards transform that compose as the identity). Notably, the proof of this orthogonality property seems to depart entirely from Yang–Baxter calculus, and rather proceeds by direct formulas that lay bare the pole structure of the participating functions.

It would be rewarding to extend as much of this framework as possible to the symmetric functions introduced in our text. Such an endeavour is likely to be extremely challenging, and would require a detailed understanding of the pole structure in the symmetrization identity (
1.8.1
) for
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
.

•

Fusion.
Arguably the most important potential follow-up to this work would be to perform fusion of the symmetric functions in question. This is a subject that is very well-developed in context of the
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{n})
series; explicit formulas for the fused
R
-matrices acting in symmetric tensor representations were obtained in
[
Man14
,
BM16
]
, and the procedure of
stochastic fusion
was developed in the works
[
CP16
,
Bor17
,
BW22
]
. This combinatorial understanding of fusion, together with explicit formulas for the weights of the fused models, allows one to readily extend results from the six-vertex model to its higher-dimensional representations. In fact, the rational symmetric functions introduced in
[
Bor17
]
were
a priori
fused in one direction (vertical lines corresponded to
\mathfrak{sl}(2)
Verma modules).

Aside from leading to a richer class of multivariate rational functions, fusion may potentially allow one to access symmetric
polynomials
as certain special limits. For example, as is well-known from the work of
[
Bor17
]
, in the limit where the weight of the underlying symmetric tensor representation tends to infinity, one recovers the classical Hall–Littlewood polynomials of type
A_{N}
. It would be interesting to investigate the same limit in the context of the
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(2)}_{2})
model.

•

Higher-rank analogues.
The IK model is just the first model in the
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(2)}_{2n})
series. The
R
-matrices of this family all have a common structure; see
[
Jim86
]
.

It would be natural to use these higher-rank analogues of the IK model to define multivariate rational functions from ensembles of
coloured
lattice paths, similarly to what was done in
[
BW22
]
in the context of
\mathcal{U}_{q}(A^{(1)}_{n})
models. It is expected that the resulting functions would be
nonsymmetric
, similarly to how the partition functions defined in
[
BW22
]
gave a nonsymmetric decomposition of the original six-vertex functions introduced in
[
Bor17
]
. Investigations along these lines would also potentially shed light on the orthogonality direction mentioned above.

1.11.
About the layout of this paper

Our text is divided into two main chapters. Chapter
2
reviews the construction of rational symmetric functions via partition functions in the six-vertex model, while Chapter
3
contains our new results on the Izergin–Korepin nineteen-vertex model.

Most of the material in Chapter
2
has appeared in previous works. The definition of the rational symmetric functions
F^{\rm 6V}_{S}
and
G^{\rm 6V}_{S}
in Section
2.3
is inherited from the
spin Hall–Littlewood functions
of
[
Bor17
]
and
[
BP16
]
: in particular, one takes a simple limit of the higher-spin vertex model in the latter papers which maps it to the stochastic six-vertex model. The Cauchy identity listed in Section
2.4
is, in turn, a special case of the skew Cauchy identities of
[
Bor17
]
and
[
BP16
]
. The stable symmetric functions
H^{\rm 6V}_{S}
and their Cauchy identity, given in Sections
2.5
–
2.6
, are closely inspired by the stable spin Hall–Littlewood functions of
[
BW21
, Section 5.3]
. Finally the symmetrization formula for
F^{\rm 6V}_{S}
in Section
2.7
is deduced as a special case of the corresponding symmetrization identity in
[
Bor17
]
and
[
BP16
]
, although our proof (based on exchange relations and Lagrange interpolation) appears to be new.

Even though Chapter
2
contains no substantive new material, we have chosen to present it as a warm-up to Chapter
3
for several reasons. The first reason is that it sets many of our notations: almost every quantity introduced in Chapter
2
has a direct analogue in Chapter
3
, and we employ common notations for these. The second reason is historical: in our investigations of the Izergin–Korepin model, the passage to many of our results was not straightforward. In several cases, it was necessary to proceed by first understanding the corresponding calculation in the six-vertex model, and we have tried to reflect this lineage in the text itself. The final reason is for the convenience of the reader: more experienced readers may prefer to read Chapters
2
and
3
in parallel, as this will immediately illustrate what aspects of the constructions are different or more complicated within the Izergin–Korepin model. Less experienced readers may prefer to read the two parts independently: both Chapters
2
and
3
are entirely self-contained, and function as standalone texts in their own right.

Chapter 2
Six-vertex model

In this chapter we study the stochastic six-vertex model in the quadrant, and review how it gives rise to a pair of rational symmetric functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
with a host of important algebraic properties.

Section
2.1
gives the definition of the stochastic six-vertex model and its intrinsic properties; we shall follow the same conventions as in
[
BW22
]
. In Section
2.2
we use the model to define row-to-row operators, and derive some of their properties. Sections
2.3
–
2.6
contain the algebraic construction of the functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
, their stable analogues
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, as well as the Cauchy identities that they satisfy.

Finally, in Section
2.7
we state and prove a symmetrization identity for
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. Although this result is not new, it is worthwhile for the reader to study this proof in some detail, as the method adopted there is ultimately employed to prove the corresponding symmetrization identity in the more complicated Izergin–Korepin model.

As we have mentioned, almost all of the results in this chapter are known (or may be deduced) from previous works, and we refer the reader to
[
Bor17
,
BP15
,
BP16
,
BW21
]
for much of the original theory.

2.1.
Definition of stochastic six-vertex model and basic relations

We begin by writing down the
R
-matrix and explain how it gives rise to a vertex model, in Section
2.1.1
. Section
2.1.2
contains the unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations of the model, and Section
2.1.3
introduces dotted analogues of the vertex weights; the latter differ from the usual vertex weights up to an overall normalization factor.

2.1.1.
R
-matrix and vertices

Definition 2.1.1
.

The
R
-matrix for the stochastic six-vertex model is a
4\times 4
matrix given by

(2.1.1)

R_{ab}(y/x)=\sum_{i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1\}}W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)E_{a}^{j,\ell}\otimes E_{b}^{i,k}

where
E_{a}^{j,\ell}
and
E_{b}^{i,k}
are
2\times 2
elementary matrices acting on the two-dimensional spaces
V_{a}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}
and
V_{b}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}
, respectively. The matrix entries satisfy the conservation property

(2.1.2)

\displaystyle W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=0,\qquad\text{if}\qquad i+j\not=k+\ell,

which leaves six possible non-vanishing choices of
(i,j;k,\ell)
. Writing the matrix (
2.1.1
) explicitly, one then finds that

(2.1.3)

R_{ab}(y/x)=\begin{bmatrix}\begin{array}[]{cccc}W_{y/x}(0,0;0,0)&0&0&0\\
0&W_{y/x}(1,0;1,0)&W_{y/x}(1,0;0,1)&0\\
0&W_{y/x}(0,1;1,0)&W_{y/x}(0,1;0,1)&0\\
0&0&0&W_{y/x}(1,1;1,1)\\
\end{array}\end{bmatrix}_{ab}

where the subscript
[\cdot]_{ab}
is used to indicate the action of
R_{ab}(y/x)
in
{\rm End}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b})
.

The non-zero matrix entries of (
2.1.3
) are identified with vertices as follows:

(2.1.4)

\qquad\text{ for }\quad i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1\},

2.1
.

Figure 2.1.
The weights of the stochastic six-vertex model.

Proposition 2.1.2

(Sum-to-unity property)
.

For any fixed
i,j\in\{0,1\}
, we have

(2.1.5)

\sum_{k=0}^{1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{1}W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=1.

Proof.

By direct verification on the vertex weights of Figure
2.1
: the rows of that figure correspond with the rows of the matrix (
2.1.3
).
∎

Remark 2.1.3
.

The sum-to-unity property (
2.1.5
) is necessary for the probabilistic interpretation of the
R
-matrix (
2.1.3
). Indeed, by making suitable choices for the parameters
x,y,q
, such as
0\leqslant y<x\leqslant 1
and
0\leqslant q\leqslant 1
, one finds that all entries of the matrix (
2.1.3
) are positive; it is thus a stochastic matrix. The stochastic property of the
R
-matrix (
2.1.3
) has been used to construct Markov processes in the quadrant in numerous prior works

[
GS92
,
BCG16
,
BP16
,
BW22
]
.

2.1.2.
Unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations

Proposition 2.1.4
.

Let
R_{ab}(x)
denote the
R
-matrix defined in equation
(
2.1.3
)
, whose components are given by (
2.1.4
) and Figure
2.1
. The
R
-matrix satisfies the unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations:

(2.1.6)

\displaystyle R_{ab}(y/x)R_{ba}(x/y)

\displaystyle={\rm id},

(2.1.7)

\displaystyle R_{ab}(y/x)R_{ac}(z/x)R_{bc}(z/y)

\displaystyle=R_{bc}(z/y)R_{ac}(z/x)R_{ab}(y/x),

where the labels
a,b,c
indicate the spaces upon which the
R
-matrix acts; here (
2.1.6
) holds as an identity in
{\rm End}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b})
, and (
2.1.7
) as an identity in
{\rm End}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c})
.

(
2.1.6
)
and
(
2.1.7
)
have the following pictorial representations:

2.1.3.
Dotted vertices

For technical reasons, in the sequel we will also require a normalized version of the weights
W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
; namely,

(2.1.10)

W^{\bullet}_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=\frac{W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)}{W_{y/x}(0,1;0,1)}=\left(\dfrac{x-qy}{x-y}\right)W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell).

To distinguish these weights from the regular ones, we shall place a dot in the center of each vertex; see Figure
2.2
.

2.2.
Row operators and the Yang–Baxter algebra

This section contains the fundamental algebraic tools that underpin most of the calculations in this chapter. In Section
2.2.1
we introduce row-operators in finite size, and list some of their commutation relations. In Section
2.2.2
we study the limit of these operators when the length of the row tends to infinity, and examine what happens to the associated commutation relations.

2.2.1.
Row operators and commutation relations

We begin by introducing the vector space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
, which is obtained by taking an
L
-fold tensor product of local spaces
V_{i}\cong\mathbb{C}^{2}
:

(2.2.1)

\mathbb{V}^{(L)}=V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{L}.

In the partition functions that we subsequently consider, each vector space
V_{i}
will correspond to a vertical lattice line; as such, the natural operators for acting on
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
are obtained by considering rows of vertices of length
L
within the model (
2.1.4
). In particular, for all
a,b\in\{0,1\}
, we define the
finite
row operator
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})\in{\rm End}(\mathbb{V}^{(L)})
as follows:

(2.2.2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z}):\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{(j_{1},\dots,j_{L})\in\{0,1\}^{L}}\left(\raisebox{-42.67912pt}{\smash{

where
(i_{1},\dots,i_{L})\in\{0,1\}^{L}
selects a fixed, arbitrary vector in
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
. The row operators
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})
depend on both the horizontal spectral parameter
x
and the vertical ones,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{L})
. However, in practice, the dependence on
\bm{z}
will have little interest for us, and we usually suppress it from our notations by writing
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})\equiv\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)
.

We shall also require a dotted version of the row operators (
2.2.2
), denoted
\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})
. These are obtained by simply replacing each vertex in (
2.2.2
) by its dotted counterpart (
2.1.10
):

(2.2.3)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z}):\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

Remark 2.2.1
.

The operators (
2.2.2
) correspond with the four entries of the
monodromy matrix
of the six-vertex model, and satisfy a collection of
2^{4}
bilinear relations known as the
Yang–Baxter algebra
. Only a few of these relations will be important for our purposes: namely, the ones that allow us to prove the symmetry of our families of multivariate functions, and their Cauchy identities. These will be discussed below.

Proposition 2.2.2
.

For any two integers
a,b\in\{0,1\}
, the operators
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)
and
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)
commute:

(2.2.4)

\displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x),\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)]=0.

Proof.

This follows from a standard Yang–Baxter argument. One begins by considering arbitrary matrix elements of the product
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)
:

\displaystyle\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}=\raisebox{-34.1433pt}{\hbox to104.31pt{\vbox to70.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-30.42924pt\lower-9.51968pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

*
are forced to assume the value
a
(by conservation of paths), and the fact that
W_{y/x}(a,a;a,a)=1
for
a\in\{0,1\}
;
cf.
the top and bottom rows of Figure
2.1
. From here, we use the Yang–Baxter equation (
2.1.9
) repeatedly to transfer the inserted
R
-matrix all the way to the right edges of the lattice:

One concludes by deleting the
R
-matrix from the right of the picture; the justification for doing so is again the fact that the edges marked
*
are frozen to the values
b
, and the trivial weight
W_{y/x}(b,b;b,b)=1
for
b\in\{0,1\}
. The net result of this calculation is the switching of horizontal lattice lines; we conclude that

\displaystyle\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

for all
(i_{1},\dots,i_{L}),(j_{1},\dots,j_{L})\in\{0,1\}^{L}
, which is precisely (
2.2.4
).
∎

Proposition 2.2.3
.

The following commutation relation holds:

(2.2.6)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(x)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y)=W_{y/x}(0,1;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y)\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(x)+W_{y/x}(1,0;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(y)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(x).

Proof.

The proof of (
2.2.6
) follows by similar reasoning to that of Proposition
2.2.2
. One again begins by considering the matrix elements of the product
\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(x)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y)
, represented as a two-row partition function, and inserting an
R
-matrix vertex at the left of the lattice (using the fact that
W_{y/x}(1,1;1,1)=1
), similarly to (
2.2.5
). This time, after repeated application of the Yang–Baxter equation, the
R
-matrix vertex emerges from the right of the picture but it cannot simply be removed modulo freezing. Rather, one must sum over the possible values of the edges which connect this vertex to the lattice, resulting in the equation

(2.2.7)

2.2.2.
Row operators in the infinite-volume limit

Before discussing the lift of our operators to rows of infinite length, we require a further definition.

Definition 2.2.4
.

An
n
-string is an infinite vector
S=(S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)
with
0\leqslant S_{i}\leqslant n
for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
, and obeying the finiteness property
\exists\ M\in\mathbb{N}
such that
S_{i}=0
for all
i>M
. Whenever
S_{i}=0
for all
i>M
, we make the identification
(S_{1},S_{2},S_{3},\dots)\equiv(S_{1},\dots,S_{M})
. We write
|S|=\sum_{i\geqslant 1}S_{i}
for the sum of components of any
n
-string and refer to this quantity as its weight. Let
\mathfrak{s}(n)
denote the set of all
n
-strings.

The functions studied in this chapter will be indexed by
1
-strings (the
n=1
case of Definition
2.2.4
). We begin by defining a suitable completion of the vector space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
, obtained by taking
L\rightarrow\infty
.
1
1

1

Equivalently, we shall work with partition functions with infinitely many vertical lines in the rightward direction.
To that end, we define

(2.2.8)

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}=\bigoplus_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}\mathbb{C}\left|S\right\rangle,

with the set
\mathfrak{s}(1)
of
1
-strings given by Definition
2.2.4
.
We shall refer to
\mathbb{V}
as the
infinite-volume limit
of the space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
.

Some care is needed to extend the action of the finite row-operators (
2.2.2
) and (
2.2.3
) to the infinite volume; indeed, one may encounter convergence issues that are not present in finite size. We shall not attempt to address this issue for all of the possible choices of row-operators, but only for the subset of them that is needed in this work. This is done in the following proposition:

Proposition 2.2.5

(
[
BP16
]
Sections 4.2 and 4.3)
.

The objects

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}_{0,0}(x),\qquad\mathcal{C}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(x),\qquad\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{1,1}(x),

are well-defined as operators in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
.

Proof.

The matrix elements of
\mathcal{A}(x)
and
\mathcal{C}(x)
are represented by one-row partition functions of the form

x
a
i_{1}
i_{2}
\dots
i_{N}
0
0
\dots
j_{1}
j_{2}
\dots
\dots
j_{N}
0
0
\dots
0
z_{1}
z_{2}
z_{N}
z_{N+1}
\dots
0
0
0

where
a\in\{0,1\}
. By virtue of the fact that
\exists\ N:i_{k}=j_{k}=0
for all
k>N
, it is clear that all vertices in this diagram past the
N
-th column must take the form
W_{z_{k}/x}(0,0;0,0)=1
. As such, viewed as operators in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
, the matrix entries of
\mathcal{A}(x)
and
\mathcal{C}(x)
consist only of finite products of rational functions.

A similar argument works for the matrix elements of
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
, which are represented by one-row partition functions using dotted vertices:

x
1
i_{1}
i_{2}
\dots
i_{N}
0
0
\dots
j_{1}
j_{2}
\dots
\dots
j_{N}
0
0
\dots
1
z_{1}
z_{2}
z_{N}
z_{N+1}
\dots
1
1
1

This time,
\exists\ N
such that all vertices past the
N
-th column must take the form
W^{\bullet}_{z_{k}/x}(0,1;0,1)=1
, and we once again conclude that entries of
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
are meaningful.
∎

Proposition 2.2.6
.

Operators
\mathcal{A}(x)
,
\mathcal{C}(x)
,
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
satisfy the following commutation relations in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
:

(2.2.9)

\displaystyle[\mathcal{A}(x),\mathcal{A}(y)]=[\mathcal{C}(x),\mathcal{C}(y)]=[\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x),\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y)]=0.

Proof.

The relations (
2.2.9
) are a direct transcription of the
(a,b)=(0,0)
,
(a,b)=(1,0)
cases of (
2.2.4
), as well as a normalized version of the
(a,b)=(1,1)
case. All of these relations survive the transition to infinite volume, in view of Proposition
2.2.5
.
∎

(
[
BP16
]
Equation (4.12))

Fix
q,x,y,z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}

for some constant
\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}
which is independent of
k
. One then has the following commutation relation in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
:

(2.2.11)

\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)\mathcal{C}(y)=\left(\frac{x-y}{x-qy}\right)\mathcal{C}(y)\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x).

Proof.

Since it will be important in what follows, we note here the version of (
2.2.6
) obtained by dividing through by
\prod_{i=1}^{L}W_{z_{i}/x}(0,1;0,1)
. This converts all row operators carrying spectral parameter
x
into their dotted counterparts:

(2.2.12)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{1,1}(x)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y)=W_{y/x}(0,1;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{1,1}(x)+W_{y/x}(1,0;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{1,0}(x).

We argue that in the limit
L\rightarrow\infty
, only the left hand side and the first term on the right hand side of (
2.2.12
) have non-vanishing matrix elements when evaluated on
\mathbb{V}
: in fact, it is clear that these terms do indeed produce (
2.2.11
) under the limit in question. Our attention then shifts to showing that matrix elements of the second term on the right hand side vanish as
L\rightarrow\infty
.

Examining the matrix elements of
\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{1,0}(x)
as
L\rightarrow\infty
, one finds that they are given by partition functions of the form

z_{1}
z_{2}
\dots
z_{N-1}
z_{N}
1
1
0
1
i_{1}
i_{2}
j_{1}
j_{2}
\dots
j_{N-1}
j_{N}
\dots
0
\dots
i_{N-1}
i_{N}
\dots
0
y
x

where as previously,
\exists\ N:i_{k}=j_{k}=0
for all
k>N
. It is then not difficult to show that all columns beyond the
N
-th one will produce pairs of vertices of the form (
2.2.10
). Since we assume that the absolute values of these quantities are uniformly bounded below
1
, and they occur infinitely often, one finds that the above partition function vanishes.
∎

2.3.
Rational symmetric functions from the six-vertex model

The goal of this section is to introduce families of multivariate rational functions, derived as partition functions in the stochastic six-vertex model. Section
2.3.1
contains the definition of the multivariate rational function
F_{S}
and Section
2.3.2
introduces its partner, the multivariate rational function
G_{S}
. Finally, in Section
2.3.3
, we prove that both functions are symmetric in their primary alphabet.

2.3.1.
Multivariate rational function
F_{S}

Definition 2.3.1
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=N
. Fix also two alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(2.3.1)

F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{C}(x_{N};\bm{z})\left|S\right\rangle,

where the row operators
\mathcal{C}(x;\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
2.2.5
, while

\left|S\right\rangle=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left|S_{k}\right\rangle_{k}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle\varnothing\right|=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\langle 0\right|_{k}

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
. We refer to
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as the primary and secondary alphabets of
F_{S}
.

Translating (
2.3.1
) into its partition function form, one has that

where all bottom incoming and right outgoing edges are assigned the state
0
. Every left incoming edge is assigned the state
1
, while top outgoing edges correspond with the entries of
S
.

Remark 2.3.2
.

The multivariate functions (
2.3.2
) are a special case of functions previously studied in
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
. The functions studied in those earlier works are more general in two ways: (a) They depend on an extra complex parameter
s
, in addition to the variables
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
q
; (b) The underlying vertex model in
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
is a
higher-spin
version of the six-vertex model, and this permits the indices on vertical lattice edges (including all
S_{i}
,
i\geqslant 1
at the top of the lattice) to take arbitrary non-negative integer values. One recovers the functions (
2.3.2
) from those of
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
by restricting each
S_{i}
,
i\geqslant 1
to lie in
\{0,1\}
, and setting
s=q^{-1/2}
.

From an alternative perspective, the functions (
2.3.2
) may be considered as
pre-fused
analogues of their higher-spin counterparts in
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
: namely, one recovers the latter objects by applying the
fusion procedure
to the former. For more information on this matter, we refer the reader to
[
BW22
, Section 3.6]
.

2.3.2.
Multivariate rational function
G_{S}

Definition 2.3.3
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=N
. Fix a further integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and two alphabets
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(2.3.3)

G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})=\left\langle 1^{N},\varnothing\right|\mathcal{A}(y_{1};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{A}(y_{M};\bm{z})\left|S\right\rangle,

where the row operators
\mathcal{A}(y_{i};\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
2.2.5
, while

\left|S\right\rangle=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left|S_{k}\right\rangle_{k}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle 1^{N},\varnothing\right|=\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N}\left\langle 1\right|_{k}\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\left\langle 0\right|_{k}\bigg)

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
. We refer to
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
and
(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as the primary and secondary alphabets of
G_{S}
.

Translating (
2.3.3
) into its partition function form, one has that

(2.3.4)

{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{135.66791pt}{-38.41646pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 187.72 -53.16)} \pgfsys@hbox{58}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

In this picture, all left incoming and right outgoing edges are assigned the state 0. The first
N
incoming bottom edges are assigned the state 1; the remaining ones are all set to 0. As in the case of the functions (
2.3.2
), the top outgoing edges correspond with the entries of
S
. We emphasize that in this definition, the number of horizontal rows,
M
, is independent of
N
.

Remark 2.3.4
.

By applying the fusion procedure to the multivariate functions (
2.3.4
), one is able to construct higher-spin analogues in which a total of
N
paths enter the lattice via its first column, with no other paths entering via the remaining columns. The functions that arise from such a procedure were also studied in the previous works
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
.

2.3.3.
Symmetry in primary alphabet

Theorem 2.3.5
.

The rational functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
, defined in
(
2.3.1
)
and
(
2.3.3
)
, are symmetric in their primary alphabets.

Proof.

The symmetry of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
follows from the commutation relation
[\mathcal{C}(x_{i};\bm{z}),\mathcal{C}(x_{j};\bm{z})]=0
for
i\not=j
; see equation (
2.2.9
). In a similar vein, the symmetry of
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
in
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
follows from the commutation relation
[\mathcal{A}(y_{i};\bm{z}),\mathcal{A}(y_{j};\bm{z})]=0
; see again (
2.2.9
).
∎

Remark 2.3.6
.

For generic
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
, neither

F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
,
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
have any symmetry properties in their secondary alphabet
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. Rather, the secondary alphabet in these functions plays an analogous role to the secondary alphabet of simpler symmetric functions, such as factorial Schur and double Grothendieck polynomials.

2.4.
Cauchy identities in the six-vertex model

In Section
2.4.1
, we state a Cauchy summation identity for the rational functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
defined in
(
2.3.1
)
and
(
2.3.3
)
. The proof of this identity is split over the subsequent sections. Section
2.4.2
introduces a further rational function
G^{\bullet}_{S}
, which is related to the original
G_{S}
via the symmetry (
2.4.7
). Making use of this alternative formulation of
G_{S}
, one is able to cast the Cauchy identity in algebraic form, and compute it using commutation relations among row operators; this is done in Section
2.4.3
. All of these ideas originally appeared in
[
Bor17
,
BP16
]
, in the setting of the higher-spin six-vertex model.

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}=\bigg|\frac{(1-qy_{j}z_{k})}{(1-y_{j}z_{k})}\cdot\frac{(x_{i}-z_{k})}{(x_{i}-qz_{k})}\bigg|<\epsilon<1,

for some constant
\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}
which is independent of
i,j,k
. For such a choice of parameters, the rational functions (
2.3.1
) and (
2.3.3
) satisfy the summation identity

(2.4.2)

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}c_{S}(q)F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})=q^{N(N+1)/2}F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}},

where the sum is taken over all
1
-strings
S
such that
|S|=N
. Here
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as usual, while
q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1}=(q^{-1}z_{1}^{-1},q^{-1}z_{2}^{-1},\dots)
.
F_{(1^{N})}
appearing on the right hand side corresponds to the function (
2.3.1
) for
S=(1^{N},0,0,\dots)
, and the constant
c_{S}(q)
is given by

(2.4.3)

c_{S}(q)=\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}q^{kS_{k}}.

The proof of Theorem
2.4.1
is deferred to Section
2.4.3
.

Remark 2.4.2
.

The quantity
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, which depends only on the variables
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
(z_{1},\dots,z_{N})
, is known as the
domain-wall partition function

[
Kor82
]
. It admits an explicit
N\times N
determinant formula
[
Ize87
]
:

(2.4.4)

\displaystyle F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\frac{\prod_{i,j=1}^{N}(x_{i}-z_{j})}{\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}(x_{i}-x_{j})(z_{j}-z_{i})}\det_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant N}\left[\frac{(1-q)z_{j}}{(x_{i}-z_{j})(x_{i}-qz_{j})}\right].

For the details of how the formula (
2.4.4
) is proved, we refer the reader to Section
2.7.4
.

2.4.2.
Flip symmetry of
G_{S}

Definition 2.4.3
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=N
. Fix a further integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and two alphabets
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(2.4.5)

G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})=\left\langle S\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1};\bm{z})\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle,

where the row operators
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{i};\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
2.2.5
, while

\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle=\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N}\left|1\right\rangle_{k}\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\left|0\right\rangle_{k}\bigg)\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle S\right|=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\langle S_{k}\right|_{k}

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
.

2.4.5
) into its partition function form, it is given by

where the quantity (
2.4.6
) is well-defined, despite the change in normalization of the underlying vertex weights. Indeed, one sees that the vertices in all columns sufficiently far to the right are frozen with weight
W^{\bullet}_{z_{j}/y_{i}}(0,1;0,1)=1
.

Proposition 2.4.4
.

Fix an integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and a
1
-string
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
such that
|S|=N
. The rational functions (
2.3.3
) and (
2.4.5
) are related under the following symmetry:

(2.4.7)

q^{-N(N+1)/2}c_{S}(q)G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})=G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z}),

where the constant
c_{S}(q)
is defined in (
2.4.3
).

Proof.

The proof is by repeated application of the local symmetry relation (
2.1.11
). To make the procedure more transparent, we begin by stating a version of (
2.1.11
) that may be applied to towers of vertices. In particular, one notes that

where
m
is an arbitrary integer. Equation (
2.4.8
) is a straightforward consequence of (
2.1.11
), combined with conservation of paths through vertices, and appropriate telescopic cancellations of factors assigned to vertical edges.

The proof concludes by taking the lattice definition (
2.4.6
) of
G^{\bullet}_{S}
and applying the relation (
2.4.8
) column by column (with
m
initially equal to
0
, and rising in value by
1
after each application of the relation). In particular, one finds that the procedure stabilizes: all indices
i,k,\ell^{\bullet}_{a}
on the right hand side of (
2.4.8
) are ultimately
0
, as one traverses sufficiently far to the right through the lattice. Keeping track of all factors acquired through this process, we read off the relation

\displaystyle G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z})=\dfrac{1}{q^{N(N+1)/2}}\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}q^{kS_{k}}G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1}),

which is precisely (
2.4.7
).
∎

2.4.3.
Proof of the Cauchy identity

We now return to the proof of Theorem
2.4.1
.

Proof.

In view of the symmetry property (
2.4.7
), to demonstrate the Cauchy identity stated in (
2.4.2
) we need to show that

(2.4.9)

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z})=F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}}.

Define an expectation value

(2.4.10)

\mathcal{E}_{N,M}=\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\dots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle.

Inserting the identity operator
\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}\left|S\right\rangle\left\langle S\right|
between the operators
\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})
on the right hand side of equation
(
2.4.10
)
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}

\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|S\right\rangle\left\langle S\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\dots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z}),

where the final line follows from the algebraic definitions (
2.3.1
) and (
2.4.5
). This matches the left hand side of (
2.4.9
).

On the other hand, commuting all
\mathcal{C}(x_{i})
and
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{j}^{-1})
operators using the relation (
2.2.11
) (noting that both the relation and convergence constraint (
2.2.10
) should be rewritten with
y\mapsto x_{i}
,
x\mapsto y_{j}^{-1}
), we find that

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\cdots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle.

We conclude by noting that

\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{j}^{-1})=\left\langle\varnothing\right|,

after which one has

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|1^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}}F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

which is precisely the right hand side of (
2.4.9
).
∎

2.5.
Stable symmetric functions

It is desirable that a basis of the ring of symmetric functions exhibits
stability
. This property describes the invariance of the functions in question when a number of variables within their alphabet are specialized appropriately. For instance, given a Schur polynomial
s_{\lambda}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
indexed by an arbitrary partition
\lambda
, setting
x_{N}=0
yields the Schur polynomial
s_{\lambda}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1})
in an alphabet of one size smaller than originally. Such a stability property allows one to extend the definition of symmetric polynomials to alphabets with infinitely many variables
[
Mac95
, Chapter I]
.

Our goal in this section is to generalize the definition (
2.3.2
) of the rational symmetric functions
F_{S}
in a way that renders them stable; this generalization results in yet another family of functions denoted
H_{S}
. These functions are defined in Section
2.5.1
, and a direct limiting procedure that constructs them is outlined in Section
2.5.2
. Their basic properties, namely their symmetry and stability, are proved in Section
2.5.4
.

2.5.1.
Multivariate rational function
H_{S}

Definition 2.5.1
.

Fix an integer
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and a vector
I=(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\in\{0,1\}^{N}
. We define the inversion number
{\rm inv}(I)
as follows:

(2.5.1)

\inv(I)=\sum_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}I_{i}(1-I_{j}).

This coincides with the usual notion of inversions, since
{\rm inv}(I)
is clearly equal to the cardinality of the set
\{a<b:I_{a}>I_{b}\}
.

Definition 2.5.2
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=K
. We introduce the rational function
H_{S}
as follows:

(2.5.2)

H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{I:|I|=K}q^{-\inv(I)}F_{S}^{I}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

with the sum taken over all vectors

I\in\{0,1\}^{N}
such that
|I|=K
, and where

(2.5.3)

Remark 2.5.3
.

The functions (

) generalize the family

. Indeed, taking

trivializes the summation on the right hand side, and one is forced to have
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})=(1^{N})
. Since
{\rm inv}(I)=0
when

, and
F_{S}^{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, one finds that
H_{S}=F_{S}
when
K=N
.

At the other extreme, when
K=0
, no particles may enter the lattice (
2.5.3
) and it freezes into a product of vertices

. We therefore have
H_{(0,0,0,\dots)}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=1
for any
N\geqslant 1
.

2.5.2.
Limiting procedure to obtain
H_{S}

Theorem 2.5.4
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
, and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=K
. Fix three alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
{\bm{u}}=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N-K})
and
{\bm{z}}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
of arbitrary parameters. The following relation then holds:

(2.5.4)

H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\frac{F_{(1^{N-K},S)}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})}{F_{(1^{N-K})}(*;\bm{u})},

where we write
\bm{u}\to\infty
as shorthand for the limits
u_{i}\rightarrow\infty
,
1\leqslant i\leqslant N-K
. The notation
(*;\bm{u})
indicates that the primary alphabet of
F_{(1^{N-K})}
may be chosen arbitrarily.

for all
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\in\{0,1\}^{N}
such that
|I|=K
. To prove equation (
2.5.6
) we require the following lemma, that allows us to incrementally modify the boundary conditions at the right edges of the partition function.

Lemma 2.5.5
.

Fix arbitrary vectors
S,T\in\{0,1\}^{N}

Proof.

Following very similar ideas to Proposition
2.2.3
, one may derive the following exchange relation between row-operators (of arbitrary length):

(2.5.8)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(x;\bm{z})\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(y;\bm{z})=\sum_{c,d:c+d=1}W_{y/x}(d,c;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,d}(y;\bm{z})\mathcal{T}_{1,c}(x;\bm{z}).

After sending
\bm{z}\rightarrow\infty
, the row operators in (
2.5.8
) become independent of their primary arguments:

(2.5.9)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{1,1}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{1,0}(*;\infty)=\sum_{c,d:c+d=1}W_{y/x}(d,c;0,1)\mathcal{T}_{1,d}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{1,c}(*;\infty),

which holds for arbitrary values of the parameter
y/x
. Consulting the weights in Figure
2.1
and sending
y/x\rightarrow\infty
, one finds that

\displaystyle W_{\infty}(d,c;0,1)=\bm{1}_{c=1}\cdot\bm{1}_{d=0}\cdot q^{-1},

and (
2.5.7
) then follows directly from (
2.5.9
).

∎

). We are therefore at liberty to choose
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})

) becomes

where the final equality follows by noting that all vertices above the red dashed line are frozen: all of these vertices have the weight

. Comparison of (
2.5.10
) and (
2.5.11
) proves (
2.5.6
), thereby completing the proof of Theorem
2.5.4
.

2.5.3.
An aside about the domain-wall partition function

We now compute the limit of the domain-wall partition function
\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}F_{(1^{N-K})}(*;\bm{u})
that surfaced throughout the computations of the previous subsection. We do this mainly for completeness, as we will not require it in the sections which follow.

Proposition 2.5.6
.

Define the following quantity:

Z_{N}(q):=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u}).

We then have the explicit evaluation

(2.5.12)

\displaystyle Z_{N}(q)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1-q^{-i}).

Proof.

When the ratio
y/x
is set to
\infty
, the weights of the
R
-matrix (
2.1.3
) become

\displaystyle W_{\infty}(0,0;0,0)=W_{\infty}(1,1;1,1)=W_{\infty}(1,0;1,0)=1,

\displaystyle W_{\infty}(1,0;0,1)=0,\quad W_{\infty}(0,1;1,0)=-\frac{1-q}{q},\quad W_{\infty}(0,1;0,1)=\frac{1}{q}.

Since
W_{\infty}(1,0;0,1)=0
, the configurations in
F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})
which survive the limit
\bm{u}\rightarrow\infty
are in bijection with the permutations of
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
. To see this, we note that the non-vanishing configurations of
F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})
have a unique vertex
W_{\infty}(0,1;1,0)
in each row and column of the lattice. Replacing each such vertex by a
1
and all other vertices by
0
, one recovers a permutation matrix
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}
(see Example
2.5.7
).

Now let us fix
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}
and compute the weight of the corresponding configuration. One finds that the frequencies of the vertices
W_{\infty}(0,1;1,0)
and
W_{\infty}(0,1;0,1)
are given by

\#_{\sigma}\{W_{\infty}(0,1;1,0)\}=N,\quad\#_{\sigma}\{W_{\infty}(0,1;0,1)\}=\binom{N}{2}-\inv(\sigma),

where
\#_{\sigma}\{W_{\infty}(i,j;k,\ell)\}
denotes the count of vertices of type
W_{\infty}(i,j;k,\ell)
within the configuration
\sigma
. Summing the weights across each configuration
\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}
we then obtain

(2.5.13)

Z_{N}(q)=(-1)^{N}(1-q)^{N}q^{-\binom{N+1}{2}}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}}q^{\inv(\sigma)}.

The sum on the right hand side is the Poincaré polynomial of
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
, which yields the factorization

(2.5.14)

(-1)^{N}(1-q)^{N}q^{-\binom{N+1}{2}}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}}q^{\inv(\sigma)}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}(1-q^{-i}),

completing the proof of (
2.5.12
).
∎
