2.5.4.
Symmetry and stability of
H_{S}

The first property of the functions
(
2.5.2
)
is their symmetry with respect to their primary alphabet:

Proposition 2.5.8
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=K
. Then the rational function
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of Theorem
2.5.4
, in view of the fact that the right hand side of (
2.5.4
) is symmetric in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.
∎

The second property is that the rational functions
(
2.5.2
)
are
stable
with respect to their primary alphabet:

Proposition 2.5.9
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=K
. We then have the reduction property

\displaystyle H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1},x_{N}=\infty;\bm{z})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\bm{z}),&\quad|S|\leqslant N-1,\\
\\
0,&\quad|S|=N.\end{array}\right.

Proof.

Since
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to its primary alphabet, we may equivalently study the limit as
x_{1}\rightarrow\infty
. This limit affects the bottommost row of vertices in the partition function (
2.5.3
). Consulting the table in Figure
2.1
, one finds that all weights
W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
have a well-defined limit as
x\rightarrow\infty
, and furthermore

(2.5.18)

\displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}W_{z/x}(0,1;1,0)=0.

It follows that
F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
vanishes if the vertex (
2.5.18
) occurs within the first row of the partition function (
2.5.3
).

Let us begin by assuming that
|S|<N
. The only way to prevent the appearance of the vertex (
2.5.18
) is to fix
I_{1}=0
, which causes the entire bottom row of the lattice to freeze away (since it is then comprised solely of
W_{0}(0,0;0,0)
vertices). As such, for any
I=(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})
we find that

\displaystyle F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\bm{1}_{I_{1}=0}\cdot F^{\tilde{I}}_{S}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),\qquad\tilde{I}=(I_{2},\dots,I_{N}),

which translates into the property

(2.5.19)

\displaystyle H_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\tilde{I}:|\tilde{I}|=K}q^{-\inv(\tilde{I})}F_{S}^{\tilde{I}}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=H_{S}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

with the sum taken over vectors

\tilde{I}=(I_{2},\dots,I_{N})
, and where the first equality in (
2.5.19
) makes use of the fact that

\displaystyle\inv(0,I_{2},\dots,I_{N})=\inv(I_{2},\dots,I_{N})=\inv(\tilde{I}).

This completes the proof of (
2.5.9
) in the case
|S|<N
.

The case
|S|=N
is handled very easily, since in this situation the vector that indexes the left incoming edges of the partition function (
2.5.3
) is forced, by conservation, to be
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})=(1^{N})
. As such, it is impossible to choose
I_{1}=0
, and
F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
vanishes identically.
∎

2.6.
Cauchy identity for stable symmetric functions

In Section
2.4
we stated a Cauchy-type identity between the rational symmetric functions
(
2.3.1
)
and
(
2.3.3
)
. Although the right hand side of the identity (
2.4.2
) may be expressed in terms of Izergin’s determinant
[
Ize87
]
, it does not fully factorize. In this section we show that the stable symmetric functions (
2.5.2
) are more natural from this point of view, and satisfy a Cauchy summation identity with a fully factorized right hand side.

Theorem 2.6.1
.

Let
N,M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
be fixed positive integers. Fix parameters
q,x_{i},y_{j},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}
such that for all
i\in\{1,\dots,N\}
,
j\in\{1,\dots,M\}
and
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the condition (
2.4.1
) holds. We then have the summation identity

(2.6.1)

\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}(-1)^{|S|}q^{MN-|S|^{2}}c_{S}(q)H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})H_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}},

where the constant
c_{S}(q)
is given by (
2.4.3
).

Proof.

Our starting point is the identity (
2.4.9
), in which we choose the secondary alphabet to be
\bm{u}\cup\bm{z}
, where
\bm{u}=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N})
and
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
:

\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})=F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}}.

Dividing this equation by
F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})
and taking the limit
\bm{u}\rightarrow\infty
, in exactly the same vein as (
2.5.4
), we read off the identity

(2.6.2)

\displaystyle\lim_{\bm{u}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})}\cdot\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{1-qx_{i}y_{j}}{1-x_{i}y_{j}},

where the right hand side of (
2.6.2
) follows from (
2.5.4
) with
S=(0,0,0,\dots)
. It remains to show that the left hand side of (
2.6.2
) matches that of (
2.6.1
).

For that purpose, we define the quantity

\displaystyle K_{N,M}:=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,

\displaystyle x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z}),

which has the graphical representation

(2.6.3)

K_{N,M}=\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\\
(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})\\
|I|=|J|\end{subarray}}
x_{1}

that have been sent to infinity, while the remaining columns correspond with the secondary alphabet
(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
that remains free. We perform summation over the vectors

and
(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})

with
\chi
defined in (
2.5.10
), and where the factor of
q^{MN}
arises from the above-mentioned normalization discrepancy between dotted and undotted vertices, while the
q
-inversions in the denominator of (
2.6.4
) are computed using the fact that

\displaystyle\inv(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})

\displaystyle=\inv(I_{1}\dots,I_{N})+\inv(J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})+|I||J|

\displaystyle=\inv(I_{1}\dots,I_{N})+\inv(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})+|I||J|.

By the invariance of
\chi
under permutation of its arguments, we may choose
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})=(0^{N},1^{M})
, which by (
2.5.11
) yields

\displaystyle\chi(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})=\chi(0^{N},1^{M})=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u}).

We have thus derived the equation

(2.6.5)

\displaystyle\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\frac{K_{N,M}}{F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})}=q^{MN}\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\\
(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})\\
|I|=|J|\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{\inv(I)+\inv(J)+|I||J|}}\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}\raisebox{-99.58464pt}{

where summation over
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
is restricted to
1
-strings such that
|S|=|I|=|J|
.

The final step is to apply a symmetry relation to the top half of the lattice on the right hand side of (
2.6.5
), similarly to that of Proposition
2.4.4
. Letting the top half of the lattice be denoted by

(2.6.6)

one may prove the relation

\displaystyle F^{\bullet J}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z})=(-1)^{|S|}c_{S}(q)F^{J}_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})

by repeated application of (
2.4.8
) to the columns of the partition function (
2.6.6
), where
c_{S}(q)
is given by (
2.4.3
) and
F^{J}_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})
by (
2.5.3
). Combining everything, we have shown that

\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\frac{K_{N,M}}{F_{(1^{N})}(*;\bm{u})}=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}(-1)^{|S|}q^{MN-|S|^{2}}c_{S}(q)\times\\
\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\\
(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})\\
|I|=|J|=|S|\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q^{\inv(I)+\inv(J)}}F^{I}_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})F^{J}_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1})\\
=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)}(-1)^{|S|}q^{MN-|S|^{2}}c_{S}(q)H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})H_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-1}\bm{z}^{-1}),

completing the proof of (
2.6.1
).
∎

2.7.
Properties of rational symmetric functions and symmetrization formula

We conclude the chapter by stating and proving a symmetrization formula for the rational symmetric functions (
2.3.1
). Our proof is based on setting up, in Sections
2.7.1
and
2.7.2
, a collection of properties which uniquely determine
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. One is then able to check that the proposed symmetrization identity, given in Section
2.7.4
, satisfies all of these properties.

2.7.1.
Exchange relations

Proposition 2.7.1
.

Fix an integer
k\geqslant 1
and a
1
-string
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
such that
S_{k}=0
and
S_{k+1}=1
. The following relation then holds:

(2.7.1)

W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(1,0;1,0)F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\\
F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})-W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(0,1;1,0)F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

where
\sigma_{k}\cdot S=(\dots,S_{k+1},S_{k},\dots)
and
\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z}=(\dots,z_{k+1},z_{k},\dots)
denote transposition of the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th elements of
S,\bm{z}
.

Proof.

The proof is by application of the Yang–Baxter equation (
2.1.9
) to the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th columns of the partition function in question.

In particular, starting from the lattice representation of
F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})
, one may attach a frozen
W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(0,0;0,0)
vertex at the base of the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th columns. By repeated application of the Yang–Baxter equation, this vertex emerges from the top of the same columns, leading to the identity

where the states assigned to external horizontal edges are arbitrary, but held fixed on both sides of the equation. Equation (
2.7.1
) then follows by rearrangement.
∎

Explicitly writing the vertex weights in (
2.7.1
), after dividing it through by
W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(1,0;1,0)
, we have

(2.7.2)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\frac{z_{k}-qz_{k+1}}{q(z_{k}-z_{k+1})}F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})-\frac{(1-q)z_{k+1}}{q(z_{k}-z_{k+1})}F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

The exchange relation (
2.7.2
) may be used repeatedly to express
F_{S}
as a linear combination of domain-wall partition functions
F_{(1^{N})}
, for arbitrary
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
.

2.7.2.
Recursion relations

Recall the definition of the domain-wall partition function
F_{(1^{N})}
; see Remark
2.4.2
. In this section we record a list of properties satisfied by this object, which determine it uniquely; these properties are originally due to Korepin
[
Kor82
]
.

Proposition 2.7.2
.

Fix an integer
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
. The domain-wall partition function
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
satisfies the following properties:

(1)

The function
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to its primary alphabet
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.

(2)

Introduce the normalized function

\tilde{F}_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{N}(x_{i}-qz_{j})F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

Then
\tilde{F}_{(1^{N})}
is a polynomial in
z_{1}
of degree
N
.

(3)

The function
F_{(1^{N})}
vanishes at
z_{1}=0
:

\displaystyle F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=0}=0.

(4)

The function
F_{(1^{N})}
has the following recursion relation with respect to
z_{1}
:

\displaystyle F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}=F_{(1^{N-1})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),

where
\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}=(z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
denotes the secondary alphabet with the omission of
z_{1}
.

(5)

In the case
N=1
we have the explicit evaluation

\displaystyle F_{(1)}(x_{1};\bm{z})=W_{z_{1}/x_{1}}(0,1;1,0)=\frac{(1-q)z_{1}}{x_{1}-qz_{1}}.

Proof.

All of the properties (1)–(5) follow directly from the partition function (
2.3.2
) under the choice
S=(1^{N},0,0,\ldots)
.

(1)

The symmetry of
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
has already been established in Theorem
2.3.5
.

(2)

Multiplying the partition function by
\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{N}(x_{i}-qz_{j})
is equivalent to converting the underlying vertex weights to their polynomial form. In particular, we define

(2.7.3)

\displaystyle\tilde{W}_{x,z}(i,j;k,\ell):=(x-qz)W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell),

which are polynomials in
x
and
z
for all
i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1\}
. The function
\tilde{F}_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is then given by the partition function setup (
2.3.2
), but using the weights (
2.7.3
). Examining this partition function, it is clear that all dependence on the parameter
z_{1}
is via the leftmost column of the lattice. Since the weights (
2.7.3
) of individual vertices in that column are degree-
1
polynomials in
z_{1}
, it is then clear that
\tilde{F}_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is a degree-
N
polynomial in
z_{1}
.

(3)

This again follows by studying the leftmost column of the partition function under consideration. It is easily seen that any configuration of this column must give rise to exactly one of the following vertex weights:

\displaystyle W_{z_{1}/x_{i}}(0,1;1,0)

\displaystyle=\frac{(1-q)z_{1}}{x_{i}-qz_{1}},

where
i
takes values in
\{1,\dots,N\}
. This weight vanishes at
z_{1}=0
, and the claim is then immediate.

(4)

Take the lattice representation of
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and use the symmetry in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
to permute the horizontal spectral parameters, so that
x_{N}
is assigned to the lowest row of the lattice, followed by
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1})
assigned to the remaining rows. In any lattice configuration, the bottom-left vertex must then take one of the following forms:

\displaystyle W_{z_{1}/x_{N}}(0,1;0,1)=\frac{x_{N}-z_{1}}{x_{N}-qz_{1}},\qquad W_{z_{1}/x_{N}}(0,1;1,0)=\frac{(1-q)z_{1}}{x_{N}-qz_{1}}.

The first of these weights vanishes at
z_{1}=x_{N}
; the second becomes
W_{1}(0,1;1,0)=1
. It is then easy to show that, after specializing
z_{1}=x_{N}
, the first row and column of
F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
freeze out entirely:

(2.7.4)

F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}=\hbox to204.88pt{\vbox to179.87pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 95.819pt\lower-29.7749pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{}{{}}{}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \color[rgb]{0.85,0.85,0.85}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.5pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}{}{}{}{{}}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -27.56 0 L -27.56 191.32}{fill:none} {{}{{}}{}{}{{}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@transformcm{0.0}{1.0}{-1.0}{0.0}{-19.91684pt}{138.2704pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform=matrix(0.0 1.0 -1.0 0.0 -27.56 191.32)} \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=1.2pt} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray=none,stroke-dashoffset=0.0pt} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linecap=round} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-linejoin=round} \lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M -3.03 4.04 C -2.78 2.53 0 0.25 0.76 0 C 0 -0.25 -2.78 -2.53 -3.03 -4.04}{fill:none} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope }}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces

The total weight of the frozen regions in (
2.7.4
) is identically
1
, and the remaining (unfrozen) portion of the lattice is simply
F_{(1^{N-1})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1})
, yielding the desired recursion.

(5)

This property is evident.

∎

2.7.3.
Proof of uniqueness

Theorem 2.7.3
.

The functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
are uniquely characterized by the exchange relations of Proposition
2.7.1
and by the properties listed in Proposition
2.7.2
.

Proof.

Suppose that
Z_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
,
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
,
|S|=N
is a family of rational functions that satisfies all of the conditions of Propositions
2.7.1
and
2.7.2
. Our task is to show that, necessarily,

(2.7.5)

\displaystyle Z_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

We begin with the observation that for any
1
-string
S
, one is able to write

(2.7.6)

\displaystyle Z_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})-F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma}d_{\sigma}^{S}\Big(Z_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma\cdot\bm{z})-F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma\cdot\bm{z})\Big),

where the sum is over permutations of the secondary alphabet
\bm{z}
, while
d_{\sigma}^{S}
are appropriate coefficients. Indeed, Proposition
2.7.1
ensures that one may write

(2.7.7)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma}d_{\sigma}^{S}F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma\cdot\bm{z})

for appropriate coefficients
d_{\sigma}^{S}
. By virtue of the assumption that
Z_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
satisfies the same exchange relations, it must then be possible to write an analogue of equation (
2.7.7
) for
Z_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
with the
same
expansion coefficients; the claim (
2.7.6
) follows immediately.

Thanks to equation (
2.7.6
), the task of proving (
2.7.5
) is reduced to showing that

(2.7.8)

\displaystyle Z_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

The rest of the proof proceeds by induction on
N
; namely, the size of the primary alphabet. Let
\mathcal{P}_{N}
denote the proposition that (
2.7.8
) holds.

We begin by noting that
\mathcal{P}_{1}
is true, by virtue of property (5). Now we proceed with the inductive hypothesis that
\mathcal{P}_{N-1}
is true for some
N\geqslant 2
, and consider the function

(2.7.9)

\displaystyle\Delta_{N}=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{N}(x_{i}-qz_{j})\Big(Z_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})-F_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big).

By property (2) of Proposition
2.7.2
,
\Delta_{N}
is a polynomial in
z_{1}
of degree
N
. The symmetry property (1), together with properties (3) and (4), specifies
\Delta_{N}
at
N+1
values of
z_{1}
. In particular, property (3) becomes
\Delta_{N}\Big|_{z_{1}=0}=0
. Property (4) becomes

\displaystyle\Delta_{N}\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{k}}=\prod_{j=2}^{N}(x_{k}-qz_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{N}(x_{i}-qx_{k})\Delta_{N-1}(x_{1},\dots,\widehat{x}_{k},\dots,x_{N};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1})=0

for all
1\leqslant k\leqslant N
, where the final equality with
0
is due to the assumption that
\mathcal{P}_{N-1}
holds. Collectively, these properties show that
\Delta_{N}
vanishes at
N+1
values of
z_{1}
; it is therefore identically zero for arbitrary
z_{1}
. Hence
\mathcal{P}_{N}
is true, and the proof is complete by induction on
N
.

∎

2.7.4.
Symmetrization formula

Definition 2.7.4
.

Fix two integers
n,N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(n)
be an
n
-string. An
n
-permutation matrix of size
N
and profile
S
is an
N\times\infty
matrix with all row sums equal to
n
, and
i
-th column sum equal to
S_{i}
for all
i\in\mathbb{N}
. We let
\mathfrak{M}_{n}(N,S)
denote the set of all such matrices.

In what follows we let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string, and denote by
\mathfrak{M}_{1}(N,S)
the set of all
1
-permutation matrices of size
N
and profile
S
. These are
N\times\infty
matrices with row sums equal to
1
, and
i
-th column sum equal to
S_{i}
for all
i\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
(see Definition
2.7.4
, above).

The rows of the matrices
\sigma\in\mathfrak{M}_{1}(N,S)
are given by unit vectors
e_{k}
, with
1
at position
k
and
0
at all remaining positions. We note that when
S=e_{k}
,
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the function (
2.3.1
) may be computed explicitly:

(2.7.10)

\displaystyle F_{e_{k}}(x;{\bm{z}})=\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\frac{x-z_{j}}{x-qz_{j}}\cdot\frac{(1-q)z_{k}}{x-qz_{k}}.

Indeed, this corresponds to the case where the partition function (
2.3.2
) consists of just a single row. One finds that it permits a unique configuration whose weight is given by a product of
k-1
vertices of the type
W_{z_{j}/x}(0,1;0,1)
and one vertex
W_{z_{k}/x}(0,1;1,0)
, which results precisely in the equation (
2.7.10
).

Theorem 2.7.5
.

Fix an integer
N\geqslant 1
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
be a
1
-string such that
|S|=N
. The rational symmetric function (
2.3.1
) is given by the explicit formula

(2.7.11)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{M}_{1}(N,S)}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\Delta_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)}(x_{i},x_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{N}F_{\sigma(i)}(x_{i};\bm{z}),

where
\sigma(i)
denotes the
i
-th row (read from top to bottom) of the
1
-permutation matrix
\sigma
, and
F_{\sigma(i)}(x_{i};\bm{z})
is given by (
2.7.10
). For any
U,V\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
such that
|U|=|V|=1
, we define

\displaystyle\Delta_{U,V}(x,y)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\dfrac{y-qx}{y-x},&\qquad\text{1 in $U$ occurs before 1 in $V$},\\
\\
\dfrac{x-qy}{x-y},&\qquad\text{1 in $U$ occurs after 1 in $V$}.\end{array}\right.

Remark 2.7.6
.

It is easy to show that (
2.7.11
) is equivalent to the more standard symmetrization identity

(2.7.12)

\displaystyle F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\frac{x_{\sigma(j)}-qx_{\sigma(i)}}{x_{\sigma(j)}-x_{\sigma(i)}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}F_{e_{k_{i}}}(x_{\sigma(i)};\bm{z}),

where
\{k_{1}<\cdots<k_{N}\}
are the coordinates of ones in the string
S
; namely,
S_{k_{i}}=1
for all
1\leqslant i\leqslant N
. The reason why we present the somewhat less natural-looking formula (
2.7.11
), rather than simply (
2.7.12
), is that the former has an immediate generalization to the setting of the Izergin–Korepin model (see Section
3.8.4
) while we do not know of any straightforward way to generalize the latter.

Proof.

Throughout the proof, we shall let

(2.7.13)

\displaystyle g_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\frac{x_{\sigma(j)}-qx_{\sigma(i)}}{x_{\sigma(j)}-x_{\sigma(i)}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}F_{e_{k_{i}}}(x_{\sigma(i)};\bm{z})

denote the right hand side of (
2.7.12
). The proof is in two steps. In the first stage, we show that
g_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
satisfies the exchange relation (
2.7.2
). In the second stage, we show that
g_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
satisfies the conditions of Proposition
2.7.2
. In view of Theorem
2.7.3
, these checks suffice to show that
g_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
for general
S\in\mathfrak{s}(1)
.

To validate the exchange relation (
2.7.2
), we fix a
1
-string
S
such that
S_{\ell}=0
,
S_{\ell+1}=1
. One finds that all factors in the sum (
2.7.13
) are symmetric in
(z_{\ell},z_{\ell+1})
and invariant under the switch
S\leftrightarrow\sigma_{\ell}\cdot S
, with the exception of the unique one-row function
F_{e_{k_{i}}}(x_{\sigma(i)};\bm{z})
, where
i
is chosen such that
k_{i}=\ell+1
. The exchange relation (
2.7.2
) is then immediately verified on this one-row function.

To check the properties of Proposition
2.7.2
, we set
S=(1^{N})
in (
2.7.13
):

(2.7.14)

\displaystyle g_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{N}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}\frac{x_{\sigma(j)}-qx_{\sigma(i)}}{x_{\sigma(j)}-x_{\sigma(i)}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}F_{e_{i}}(x_{\sigma(i)};\bm{z}).

(1)

The symmetry in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
is manifest from of (
2.7.14
).

(2)

Multiplying (
2.7.14
) by
\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{N}(x_{i}-qz_{j})
converts each factor
F_{e_{i}}(x_{\sigma(i)};\bm{z})
to a degree-
1
polynomial in
z_{1}
. Hence the renormalized version of (
2.7.14
) itself is a polynomial in
z_{1}
of degree
N
.

(3)

The function
F_{e_{1}}(x_{\sigma(1)};\bm{z})
vanishes at
z_{1}=0
, and the vanishing of (
2.7.14
) at the same point is then immediate.

(4)

The functions
F_{e_{i}}(x_{N};\bm{z})
,
2\leqslant i\leqslant N
all vanish at
z_{1}=x_{N}
. Setting
z_{1}=x_{N}
in (
2.7.14
), we are then forced to have
\sigma(1)=N
. Writing
(\sigma(2),\dots,\sigma(N))=(\rho(1),\dots,\rho(N-1))\in\mathfrak{S}_{N-1}
for the remaining elements of the permutation
\sigma
, one finds that

(2.7.15)

g_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}=\\
\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}\frac{x_{j}-qx_{N}}{x_{j}-x_{N}}F_{e_{1}}(x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}\times\sum_{\rho\in\mathfrak{S}_{N-1}}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N-1}\frac{x_{\rho(j)}-qx_{\rho(i)}}{x_{\rho(j)}-x_{\rho(i)}}\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}F_{e_{i+1}}(x_{\rho(i)};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}.

The recursion
g_{(1^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}=g_{(1^{N-1})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1})
then follows after using the fact that

\displaystyle F_{e_{i+1}}(x_{\rho(i)};\bm{z})=\frac{x_{\rho(i)}-z_{1}}{x_{\rho(i)}-qz_{1}}F_{e_{i}}(x_{\rho(i)};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),\qquad\forall\ 1\leqslant i\leqslant N-1,

which is an immediate consequence of the definition (
2.7.10
).

(5)

For
N=1
, the summation over
\mathfrak{S}_{N}
is trivial, and one sees that
g_{(1)}(x_{1};\bm{z})=F_{e_{1}}(x_{1};\bm{z})=F_{(1)}(x_{1};\bm{z})
.

∎

Remark 2.7.7
.

Just as we did throughout the previous proof, one may also show that the determinant formula (
2.4.4
) satisfies the properties of Proposition
2.7.2
; indeed, this was its original proof due to Izergin
[
Ize87
]
. Outside of showing that they obey the same set of uniquely-characterizing properties, we do not know of a direct way to relate the formulas (
2.4.4
) and (
2.7.12
) at
S=(1^{N})
.

Chapter 3
Nineteen-vertex model

This chapter contains the main results of our text. We introduce two families of rational symmetric functions arising from the

R
-matrix of the Izergin–Korepin nineteen-vertex model
[
IK81
,
Jim86
,
LS99
]
and study a number of their properties. Where possible, our constructions proceed directly in parallel with those of the six-vertex model and employ common notations. While this does create a double-usage of many symbols and functions, we believe that there is no potential for confusion due to the partitioning of our text into chapters.

In Section
3.1
, we write down the
R
-matrix of the model in a certain choice of gauge differing from the one in
[
Jim86
]
: our choice endows the
R
-matrix with a sum-to-unity property, namely, all of its rows sum to
1
. We state the Yang–Baxter equation and the unitarity relation for our
R
-matrix. In analogy with the six-vertex model, we also define dotted vertices (obtained as normalizations of undotted ones) and observe a symmetry between the dotted and undotted vertices.

In Section
3.2
we introduce row operators for the model, and in Section
3.3
we use them to construct the rational functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
. Key properties of these functions, including their symmetry in their (primary) alphabet and Cauchy identity, are proved in Sections
3.3
and
3.4
. In analogy with the six-vertex model, the Cauchy identity obtained at this point does not have a factorized right hand side: rather, one sees the appearance of the domain-wall partition function of the Izergin–Korepin model, previously studied in
[
Gar16
]
.

Subsequently, in Sections
3.5
–
3.6
we introduce a further family of rational symmetric functions
H_{S}
(which have a stability property with respect to their primary alphabet) and offer a simplified version of the Cauchy identity with a fully factorized right hand side. The proof of these facts rests on demonstrating how to degenerate both the functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
to
H_{S}
.

By far the most challenging result of the chapter, and indeed of the whole text, is contained in Sections
3.7
–
3.8
: we present a symmetrization formula for the family of symmetric functions
F_{S}
. This formula is conceptually very similar to its six-vertex analogue in Section
2.7
, in the sense that it expresses
F_{S}
as a sum over products of one-variable wavefunctions, dressed by appropriate two-variable scattering factors. However, the proof of this formula ends up being far more involved than in the six-vertex case. The crux of the difficulty may be seen by analysing the weights of the Izergin–Korepin vertex model: once normalized to be polynomials, one finds that they are typically of degree-two in their spectral parameters, rather than degree-one as in the six-vertex case. This means that any type of Lagrange interpolation proof necessarily requires twice the number of interpolating points as previously; this creates technical problems both for setting up the required recursion relations and for validating them on the formula itself.

3.1.
Definition of Izergin–Korepin nineteen-vertex model and basic relations

We begin by writing down the
R
-matrix and explain how it gives rise to a vertex model, in Section
3.1.1
. Section
3.1.2
contains the unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations of the model, and Section
3.1.3
introduces dotted analogues of the vertex weights.

3.1.1.
R
-matrix and vertices

Definition 3.1.1
.

The
R
-matrix for the Izergin–Korepin model is a
9\times 9
matrix given by

(3.1.1)

R_{ab}(y/x)=\sum_{i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1,2\}}W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)E_{a}^{j,\ell}\otimes E_{b}^{i,k}

where
E_{a}^{j,\ell}
and
E_{b}^{i,k}
are
3\times 3
elementary matrices acting on the three–dimensional spaces
V_{a}\cong\mathbb{C}^{3}
and
V_{b}\cong\mathbb{C}^{3}
, respectively. The matrix entries
W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
are identified with vertices as follows:

(3.1.2)

j
\ell
i
k
x
y
W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=
\qquad\text{ for }\quad i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1,2\},

where the arguments
(i,j;k,\ell)
are read in clockwise manner around the vertex. The vertex weights satisfy the conservation property

(3.1.3)

\displaystyle W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=0,\qquad\text{if}\qquad i+j\not=k+\ell,

which leaves nineteen possible non-vanishing choices of
(i,j;k,\ell)
. We tabulate all of these possibilities, together with their explicit weights, in Figure
3.1
.

Remark 3.1.2
.

While the
R
-matrix for the Izergin–Korepin model has nineteen non-vanishing weights, it is crucial to differentiate it from the nineteen-vertex Zamolodchikov–Fateev model
[
ZF80
,
LS99
]
, which is derived from fusion of the six-vertex model. Indeed, if one were to work with the latter model, most results could be obtained from suitable fusion of results in Chapter
2
. The nineteen-vertex Izergin–Korepin model does not afford us such a luxury.

It should also be emphasized that the vertices (
3.1.2
) are
not
coloured
1
1

1

In other words, arising from the quantized affine Lie algebra
\mathcal{U}_{q}(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}})
.
variants of the six-vertex model, as were studied in
[
BW22
]
. Instead, the states attached to each edge denote the
total number
of paths present, and the conservation property (
3.1.3
) means that the total flux of paths through a vertex is preserved. This approach contrasts with coloured vertex models, where edge labels indicate the
colour
of the path present, rather than the quantity.

Remark 3.1.3
.

The model presented in Figure
3.1
may seem intimidating at first glance, but it should be noted that in practical calculations one usually only needs explicit knowledge of a subset of the vertex weights. For example, for the purpose of deriving the symmetry of our functions and their Cauchy identities (see Sections
3.3
and
3.4
), it turns out that only explicit knowledge of the weights

\displaystyle W_{y/x}(0,0;0,0)=1,\qquad W_{y/x}(2,2;2,2)=1,\qquad W_{y/x}(0,2;0,2)=\dfrac{(x-y)(x-qy)}{(x-q^{2}y)(x-q^{3}y)}

is needed; the remaining weights are implicitly treated as providing a solution to the Yang–Baxter equation.

A further nice aspect of the model in Figure
3.1
is that two copies of the six-vertex model are embedded within it. Indeed, if one restricts to
(i,j;k,\ell)
such that
0\leqslant i+j\leqslant 1
or
3\leqslant i+j\leqslant 4
, one finds that the resulting weights
W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
match with six-vertex weights, up to replacing
q
in the latter model by
q^{2}
.

Proposition 3.1.4

(Sum-to-unity property)
.

For any fixed
i,j\in\{0,1,2\}
, we have

(3.1.4)

\sum_{k=0}^{2}\sum_{\ell=0}^{2}W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=1.

Proof.

This is by direct verification, using the weights in Figure
3.1
. Indeed, each row of that figure has fixed values for the incoming indices
i,j
, meaning that one simply sums the weights along each row to deduce the result.
∎

3.1.2.
Unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations

Proposition 3.1.6
.

Let
R_{ab}(x)
denote the
R
-matrix defined in equation
(
3.1.1
)
, whose components are given by (
3.1.2
) and Figure
3.1
. The
R
-matrix satisfies the unitarity and Yang–Baxter relations:

(3.1.5)

\displaystyle R_{ab}(y/x)R_{ba}(x/y)

\displaystyle={\rm id},

(3.1.6)

\displaystyle R_{ab}(y/x)R_{ac}(z/x)R_{bc}(z/y)

\displaystyle=R_{bc}(z/y)R_{ac}(z/x)R_{ab}(y/x),

where the labels
a,b,c
indicate the spaces upon which the
R
-matrix acts; here (
3.1.5
) holds as an identity in
{\rm End}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b})
, and (
3.1.6
) as an identity in
{\rm End}(V_{a}\otimes V_{b}\otimes V_{c})
.

3.1.3.
Dotted vertices

For technical reasons, in the sequel we will also require a normalized version of the weights
W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
; namely,

(3.1.9)

W^{\bullet}_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=\dfrac{W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)}{W_{y/x}(0,2;0,2)}=\dfrac{(x-q^{2}y)(x-q^{3}y)}{(x-y)(x-qy)}W_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell).

By analogy with the six-vertex model, we place dots in the center of each vertex
(
3.1.2
)
to denote the normalized weight
W^{\bullet}_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
.

It is clear that the normalized weights (
3.1.9
) continue to satisfy the Yang–Baxter equation (
3.1.8
) as written. However, (
3.1.7
) is not scale-invariant and its right hand side needs to be appropriately normalized in order for the equation to be valid for dotted vertices.

Proposition 3.1.7
.

The vertices presented in equation
(
3.1.9
)
can be related to those of equation
(
3.1.2
)
under
x\mapsto x^{-1}
and
y\mapsto q^{-3}y^{-1}
, via the following symmetry:

(3.1.10)

W^{\bullet}_{y/x}(i,j;k,\ell)=q^{2j^{\bullet}}(q-1)^{\bm{1}_{k=1}-\bm{1}_{i=1}}(-q)^{\bm{1}_{k=2}-\bm{1}_{i=2}}W_{x/y/q^{3}}(k,j^{\bullet};i,\ell^{\bullet})\quad\text{ for all }\quad i,j,k,\ell\in\{0,1,2\},

where
j^{\bullet}=2-j
and
\ell^{\bullet}=2-\ell
. Pictorially, the vertices are related in the following way:

(3.1.11)

i
k
j
\ell
x
y
=
k
i
j^{\bullet}
\ell^{\bullet}
x^{-1}
q^{-3}y^{-1}
\times\ \ q^{2j^{\bullet}}(q-1)^{\bm{1}_{k=1}-\bm{1}_{i=1}}(-q)^{\bm{1}_{k=2}-\bm{1}_{i=2}}.

Proof.

Equation
(
3.1.10
)
can be checked directly on each individual vertex.
∎

3.2.
Row operators and the Yang–Baxter algebra

This section contains the fundamental algebraic tools that underpin most of the calculations in this chapter. In Section
3.2.1
we introduce row-operators in finite size, and list some of their commutation relations. In Section
3.2.2
we study the limit of these operators when the length of the row tends to infinity, and examine what happens to the associated commutation relations.

3.2.1.
Row operators and commutation relations

We begin by introducing the vector space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
, which is obtained by taking an
L
-fold tensor product of local spaces
V_{i}\cong\mathbb{C}^{3}
:

(3.2.1)

\mathbb{V}^{(L)}=V_{1}\otimes V_{2}\otimes\cdots\otimes V_{L}.

In the partition functions that we subsequently consider, each vector space
V_{i}
will correspond to a vertical lattice line; as such, the natural operators for acting on
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
are obtained by considering rows of vertices of length
L
within the model (
3.1.2
). In particular, for all
a,b\in\{0,1,2\}
, we define the
finite
row operator
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})\in{\rm End}(\mathbb{V}^{(L)})
as follows:

(3.2.2)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z}):\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{(j_{1},\dots,j_{L})\in\{0,1,2\}^{L}}\left(\raisebox{-42.67912pt}{\smash{

where
(i_{1},\dots,i_{L})\in\{0,1,2\}^{L}
selects a fixed, arbitrary vector in
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
. The row operators
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})
depend on both the horizontal spectral parameter
x
and the vertical ones,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{L})
. However, in practice, the dependence on
\bm{z}
will have little interest for us, and we usually suppress it from our notations by writing
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})\equiv\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)
.

We shall also require a dotted version of the row operators (
3.2.2
), denoted
\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z})
. These are obtained by simply replacing each vertex in (
3.2.2
) by its dotted counterpart (
3.1.9
):

(3.2.3)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{a,b}(x;\bm{z}):\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{(j_{1},\dots,j_{L})\in\{0,1,2\}^{L}}\left(\raisebox{-42.67912pt}{\smash{

{{}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{}{}{{

Remark 3.2.1
.

The operators (
3.2.2
) correspond with the nine entries of the
monodromy matrix
of the Izergin–Korepin model, and satisfy a collection of
3^{4}
bilinear relations known as the
Yang–Baxter algebra
. Only a few of these relations will be important for our purposes: namely, the ones that allow us to prove the symmetry of our families of multivariate functions, and their Cauchy identities. These will be discussed below.

Proposition 3.2.2
.

For any two integers
a,b\in\{0,2\}
, the operators
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)
and
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)
commute:

(3.2.4)

\displaystyle[\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x),\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)]=0.

Proof.

This follows from a standard Yang–Baxter argument. One begins by considering arbitrary matrix elements of the product
\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)
:

\displaystyle\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}=\raisebox{-34.1433pt}{\hbox to104.31pt{\vbox to70.26pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip-30.42924pt\lower-9.51968pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}

*

a
(by conservation of paths), and the fact that
W_{y/x}(a,a;a,a)=1

a\in\{0,2\}
;
cf.
the top and bottom rows of Figure
3.1
. From here, we use the Yang–Baxter equation (
3.1.8
) repeatedly to transfer the inserted
R
-matrix all the way to the right edges of the lattice:

One concludes by deleting the
R
-matrix from the right of the picture; the justification for doing so is again the fact that the edges marked
*
are frozen to the values
b
, and the trivial weight
W_{y/x}(b,b;b,b)=1
for
b\in\{0,2\}
. The net result of this calculation is the switching of horizontal lattice lines; we conclude that

\displaystyle\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left\langle j_{k}\right|_{k}\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(y)\mathcal{T}_{a,b}(x)\bigotimes_{k=1}^{L}\left|i_{k}\right\rangle_{k}

for all
(i_{1},\dots,i_{L}),(j_{1},\dots,j_{L})\in\{0,1,2\}^{L}
, which is precisely (
3.2.4
).
∎

Remark 3.2.3
.

It is worth mentioning that Proposition
3.2.2
cannot be extended to the situation where
a,b
take the value
1
. The point where the reasoning breaks is that in the Izergin–Korepin model, a vertex whose incoming states both assume the value
1
is
not
forced to have outgoing states both equal to
1
; see, in particular, the middle row of Figure
3.1
. This lack of freezing prevents one from freely attaching/detaching an
R
-matrix vertex as in the previous argument.

Proposition 3.2.4
.

The following commutation relation holds:

(3.2.6)

\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(x)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(y)=\\
W_{y/x}(0,2;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(y)\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(x)+W_{y/x}(1,1;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(y)\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(x)+W_{y/x}(2,0;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(y)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(x).

Proof.

The proof of
(
3.2.6
)
follows by similar reasoning to that of Proposition
3.2.2
. One again begins by considering the matrix elements of the product
\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(x)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(y)
, represented as a two-row partition function, and inserting an
R
-matrix vertex at the left of the lattice (using the fact that
W_{y/x}(2,2;2,2)=1
), similarly to (
3.2.5
). This time, after repeated application of the Yang–Baxter equation, the
R
-matrix vertex emerges from the right of the picture but it cannot simply be removed modulo freezing. Rather, one must sum over all possible values of the edges which connect this vertex to the lattice, resulting in the equation

(3.2.7)

3.2.2.
Row operators in the infinite-volume limit

Our main interest in this work is not the vector space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
, but rather a suitable completion of it obtained by taking
L\rightarrow\infty
.
2
2

2

Equivalently, we shall work with partition functions with infinitely many vertical lines in the rightward direction.
To that end, we define

(3.2.8)

\displaystyle\mathbb{V}=\bigoplus_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}\mathbb{C}\left|S\right\rangle,

where we recall the set
\mathfrak{s}(2)
of
2
-strings given in Definition
2.2.4
.
We refer to
\mathbb{V}
as the
infinite-volume limit
of the space
\mathbb{V}^{(L)}
.

Some care is needed to extend the action of the finite row-operators (
3.2.2
) and (
3.2.3
) to the infinite volume; indeed, one may encounter convergence issues that are not present in finite size. We shall not attempt to address this issue for all of the possible choices of row-operators, but only for the subset of them that is needed in this work. This is done in the following proposition:

Proposition 3.2.5
.

The objects

\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}_{0,0}(x),\qquad\mathcal{C}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(x),\qquad\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x):=\lim_{L\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,2}(x),

are well-defined as operators in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
.

Proof.

The matrix elements of
\mathcal{A}(x)
and
\mathcal{C}(x)
are represented by one-row partition functions of the form

x
a
i_{1}
i_{2}
\dots
i_{N}
0
0
\dots
j_{1}
j_{2}
\dots
\dots
j_{N}
0
0
\dots
0
z_{1}
z_{2}
z_{N}
z_{N+1}
\dots
0
0
0

where
a\in\{0,2\}
. By virtue of the fact that
\exists\ N:i_{k}=j_{k}=0
for all
k>N
, it is clear that all vertices in this diagram past the
N
-th column must take the form
W_{z_{k}/x}(0,0;0,0)=1
. As such, viewed as operators in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
, the matrix entries of
\mathcal{A}(x)
and
\mathcal{C}(x)
consist only of finite products of rational functions.

A similar argument works for the matrix elements of
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
, which are represented by one-row partition functions using dotted vertices:

x
2
i_{1}
i_{2}
\dots
i_{N}
0
0
\dots
j_{1}
j_{2}
\dots
\dots
j_{N}
0
0
\dots
2
z_{1}
z_{2}
z_{N}
z_{N+1}
\dots
2
2
2

This time,
\exists\ N
such that all vertices past the
N
-th column must take the form
W^{\bullet}_{z_{k}/x}(0,2;0,2)=1
, and we once again conclude that entries of
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
are meaningful.
∎

Proposition 3.2.6
.

Operators
\mathcal{A}(x)
,
\mathcal{C}(x)
,
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)
satisfy the following commutation relations in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
:

(3.2.9)

\displaystyle[\mathcal{A}(x),\mathcal{A}(y)]=[\mathcal{C}(x),\mathcal{C}(y)]=[\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x),\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y)]=0.

Proof.

The relations (
3.2.9
) are a direct transcription of the
(a,b)=(0,0)
,
(a,b)=(2,0)
cases of (
3.2.4
), as well as a normalized version of the
(a,b)=(2,2)
case. All of these relations survive the transition to infinite volume, in view of Proposition
3.2.5
.
∎

\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}=\bigg|\frac{(x-q^{2}z_{k})(x-q^{3}z_{k})}{(x-z_{k})(x-qz_{k})}\cdot\frac{(y-z_{k})(y-qz_{k})}{(y-q^{2}z_{k})(y-q^{3}z_{k})}\bigg|<\epsilon<1,

for some constant
\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}
which is independent of
k
. One then has the following commutation relation in
{\rm End}(\mathbb{V})
:

(3.2.12)

\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x)\mathcal{C}(y)=\frac{(x-y)(x-qy)}{(x-q^{2}y)(x-q^{3}y)}\mathcal{C}(y)\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(x).

Proof.

Since it will be important in what follows, we note here the version of (
3.2.6
) obtained by dividing through by
\prod_{i=1}^{L}W_{z_{i}/x}(0,2;0,2)
. This converts all row operators carrying spectral parameter
x
into their dotted counterparts:

(3.2.13)

\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,2}(x)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(y)=\\
W_{y/x}(0,2;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,2}(x)+W_{y/x}(1,1;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,1}(x)+W_{y/x}(2,0;0,2)\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,0}(x).

We argue that in the limit
L\rightarrow\infty
, only the left hand side and the first term on the right hand side of (
3.2.13
) have non-vanishing matrix elements when evaluated on
\mathbb{V}
: in fact, it is clear that these terms do indeed produce (
3.2.12
) under the limit in question. Our attention then shifts to showing that matrix elements of the second and third terms on the right hand side vanish as
L\rightarrow\infty
.

Examining the matrix elements of
\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,1}(x)
and
\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(y)\mathcal{T}^{\bullet}_{2,0}(x)
as
L\rightarrow\infty
, one finds that they are given by partition functions of the form

3.3.
Rational symmetric functions from the nineteen-vertex model

The goal of this section is to introduce families of multivariate rational functions, derived as partition functions in the Izergin–Korepin model. Our approach is closely inspired by that of Section
2.3
for the six-vertex model.
Section
3.3.1
contains the definition of the multivariate rational function
F_{S}
and Section
3.3.2
introduces its partner, the multivariate rational function
G_{S}
. Finally, in Section
3.3.3
, we prove that both functions are symmetric in their primary alphabet.

3.3.1.
Multivariate rational function
F_{S}

Definition 3.3.1
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2N
. Fix also two alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(3.3.1)

F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{C}(x_{N};\bm{z})\left|S\right\rangle,

where the row operators

\mathcal{C}(x_{i};\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
3.2.5
, while

\left|S\right\rangle=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left|S_{k}\right\rangle_{k}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle\varnothing\right|=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\langle 0\right|_{k}

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
. We refer to
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
and
(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as the primary and secondary alphabets of
F_{S}
.

Translating (
3.3.1
) into its partition function form, one has that

(3.3.2)

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

where all bottom incoming and right outgoing edges are assigned the state
0
. Every left incoming edge is assigned the state
2
, while top outgoing edges correspond with the entries of
S
. The object (
3.3.2
) is to be interpreted as a partition function in the statistical mechanical sense: one works out all possible labelling of internal lattice edges and assigns a weight to each such configuration, which is the product of all individual vertices (
3.1.2
) that comprise it. Summing these weights across all possible configurations yields the rational function
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
.

Remark 3.3.2
.

A key difference between the rational functions
(
3.3.2
)
and their six-vertex counterparts
(
2.3.2
)
lies in the alteration of the states on the left of the lattice: these all assume the value
2
, rather than
1
as in the six-vertex case. Paths continue to enter from the left and exit towards the top of the lattice; however, in the Izergin–Korepin model there is increased freedom, as pairs of paths can now split and recombine multiple times under the weights
W_{z/x}(0,2;1,1)
,
W_{z/x}(2,0;1,1)
,
W_{z/x}(1,1;0,2)
,
W_{z/x}(1,1;2,0)
. As such, the functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
contain many more non-trivial configurations than their six-vertex cousins.

Remark 3.3.3
.

Since the index of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is a
2
-string, there exists an integer
M
such that
S_{k}=0
for all
k>M
. It is then straightforward to see that all columns to the right of column
M
freeze in the partition function (
3.3.2
): they are comprised solely of vertices
W_{z_{k}/x_{i}}(0,0;0,0)
which have weight
1
. In view of this fact, it is often convenient to identify the function (
3.3.2
) with the following finite-lattice version:

3.3.2.
Multivariate rational function
G_{S}

Definition 3.3.5
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2N
. Fix a further integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and two alphabets
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(3.3.4)

G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})=\left\langle 2^{N},\varnothing\right|\mathcal{A}(y_{1};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{A}(y_{M};\bm{z})\left|S\right\rangle,

where the row operators
\mathcal{A}(y_{i};\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
3.2.5
, while

\left|S\right\rangle=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left|S_{k}\right\rangle_{k}\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle 2^{N},\varnothing\right|=\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N}\left\langle 2\right|_{k}\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\left\langle 0\right|_{k}\bigg)

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
. We refer to
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
and
(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as the primary and secondary alphabets of
G_{S}
.

Translating (
3.3.4
) into its partition function form, one has that

3.3.3.
Symmetry in primary alphabet

Below we present our first main result of the chapter.

Theorem 3.3.7
.

The rational functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
and
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
, defined in
(
3.3.1
)
and
(
3.3.4
)
, are symmetric in their primary alphabets.

Proof.

The symmetry of
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
follows from the commutation relation
[\mathcal{C}(x_{i};\bm{z}),\mathcal{C}(x_{j};\bm{z})]=0
for
i\not=j
; see equation (
3.2.9
). In a similar vein, the symmetry of
G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})
in
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
follows from the commutation relation
[\mathcal{A}(y_{i};\bm{z}),\mathcal{A}(y_{j};\bm{z})]=0
; see again (
3.2.9
).
∎

3.4.
Cauchy identities in the nineteen-vertex model

In Section
3.4.1
, we state a Cauchy summation identity for the rational functions
F_{S}
and
G_{S}
defined in
(
3.3.1
)
and
(
3.3.4
)
. The proof of this identity is split over the subsequent sections, and closely follows ideas from the proof of the Cauchy identity in the six-vertex model. In particular, Section
3.4.2
introduces a further rational function
G^{\bullet}_{S}
, which is related to the original
G_{S}
via the symmetry (
3.4.7
). Making use of this alternative formulation of
G_{S}
, one is able to cast the Cauchy identity in algebraic form, and compute it using commutation relations among row operators; this is done in Section
3.4.3
.

3.4.1.
Cauchy identity

Definition 3.4.1

(Counting function)
.

For each
2
-string
S=(S_{1},S_{2},\dots)
and integer
1\leqslant i\leqslant 2
, define the counting function
\mathfrak{c}_{i}(S)
to be multiplicity of
i
in
S
; namely,
\mathfrak{c}_{i}(S)={\rm Card}\{j:S_{j}=i\}
.

Theorem 3.4.2
.

Let
N,M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
be fixed positive integers. Fix parameters

such that for all

,
j\in\{1,\dots,M\}
and
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the following conditions hold:

\lxSVG@closescope
\lxSVG@closescope {{
{}{}{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}=\bigg|\frac{(1-q^{2}y_{j}z_{k})(1-q^{3}y_{j}z_{k})}{(1-y_{j}z_{k})(1-qy_{j}z_{k})}\cdot\frac{(x_{i}-z_{k})(x_{i}-qz_{k})}{(x_{i}-q^{2}z_{k})(x_{i}-q^{3}z_{k})}\bigg|<\epsilon<1,

for some constant
\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}
which is independent of
i,j,k
. For such a choice of parameters, the rational functions (
3.3.1
) and (
3.3.4
) satisfy the summation identity

(3.4.3)

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}c_{S}(q)F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1})\\
=q^{N(2N+1)}F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})},

where the sum is taken over all
2
-strings
S
such that
|S|=2N
. Here
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
as usual, while
q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1}=(q^{-3}z_{1}^{-1},q^{-3}z_{2}^{-1},\dots)
.
F_{(2^{N})}
appearing on the right hand side corresponds to the function (
3.3.1
) for
S=(2^{N},0,0,\dots)
, and the constant
c_{S}(q)
is given by

(3.4.4)

c_{S}(q)=(-1)^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)/2}(1-q)^{-\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)}q^{-\mathfrak{c}_{2}(S)}\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}q^{2kS_{k}}.

The proof of Theorem
3.4.2
is deferred to Section
3.4.3
.

Remark 3.4.3
.

As with the corresponding Cauchy identity (
2.4.2
) in the six-vertex case, one again sees the appearance of a domain-wall-type partition function on the right hand side of (
3.4.3
). In contrast to the six-vertex case, however, there is no known determinant formula for
F_{(2^{N})}
other than when the parameter
q
is set to a root of unity
[
Gar16
]
.

3.4.2.
Flip symmetry of
G_{S}

In a similar vein to the six-vertex model, we introduce here the rational function
G^{\bullet}_{S}
, which will play a key role in the proof of the Cauchy identity (
3.4.3
).

Definition 3.4.4
.

Fix
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2N
. Fix a further integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and two alphabets
(y_{1},\dots,y_{M})
,
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
. We define the multivariate rational function

(3.4.5)

G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};\bm{z})=\left\langle S\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M};\bm{z})\cdots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1};\bm{z})\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle,

where the row operators
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{i};\bm{z})
are given by Proposition
3.2.5
, while

\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle=\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N}\left|2\right\rangle_{k}\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{k=N+1}^{\infty}\left|0\right\rangle_{k}\bigg)\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle S\right|=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{\infty}\left\langle S_{k}\right|_{k}

denote states in
\mathbb{V}
and its dual
\mathbb{V}^{*}
.

Translating (
3.4.5
) into its partition function form, it is given by

(3.4.6)

3.4.6
) is well-defined, despite the change in normalization of the underlying vertex weights. Indeed, one sees that the vertices in all columns sufficiently far to the right are frozen with weight
W^{\bullet}_{z_{j}/y_{i}}(0,2;0,2)=1
.

Proposition 3.4.5
.

Fix an integer
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and a
2
-string
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
such that
|S|=2N
. The rational functions (
3.3.4
) and (
3.4.5
) are related under the following symmetry:

(3.4.7)

q^{-N(2N+1)}c_{S}(q)G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1})=G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z}),

where the constant
c_{S}(q)
is defined in
(
3.4.4
)
.

Proof.

The proof is by repeated application of the local symmetry relation (
3.1.10
). To make the procedure more transparent, we begin by stating a version of (
3.1.10
) that may be applied to towers of vertices. In particular, one notes that

where
m
is an arbitrary integer. Equation (
3.4.8
) is a straightforward consequence of (
3.1.10
), combined with conservation of paths through vertices, and appropriate telescopic cancellations of factors assigned to vertical edges.

The proof concludes by taking the lattice definition (
3.4.6
) of
G^{\bullet}_{S}
and applying the relation (
3.4.8
) column by column (with
m
initially equal to
0
, and rising in value by
2
after each application of the relation). In particular, one finds that the procedure stabilizes: all indices
i,k,\ell^{\bullet}_{a}
on the right hand side of (
3.4.8
) are ultimately
0
, as one traverses sufficiently far to the right through the lattice. Keeping track of all factors acquired through this process, we read off the relation

(3.4.9)

\displaystyle G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z})=\dfrac{(-1)^{N}}{q^{N(2N+1)}(q-1)^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)}(-q)^{\mathfrak{c}_{2}(S)}}\prod_{k=1}^{\infty}q^{2kS_{k}}G_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1}).

Noting that for any
2
-string
S
such that
|S|=2N
one has

\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)+\mathfrak{c}_{2}(S)=\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)}{2}+\frac{|S|}{2}=\frac{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(S)}{2}+N,

we may rearrange signs in (
3.4.9
) to recover (
3.4.7
).
∎

3.4.3.
Proof of the Cauchy identity

We now return to the proof of Theorem
3.4.2
.

Proof.

In view of the symmetry property (
3.4.7
),
to demonstrate the Cauchy identity stated in
(
3.4.3
)
we need to show that

(3.4.10)

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z})=F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})}.

Define an expectation value

(3.4.11)

\mathcal{E}_{N,M}=\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\dots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle.

Inserting the identity operator
\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}\left|S\right\rangle\left\langle S\right|
between the operators
\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})
on the right hand side of equation
(
3.4.11
)
, we obtain

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}

\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|S\right\rangle\left\langle S\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\dots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{z}),

where the final line follows from the algebraic definitions (
3.3.1
) and (
3.4.5
). This matches the left hand side of (
3.4.10
).

On the other hand, commuting all
\mathcal{C}(x_{i})
and
\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{j}^{-1})
operators using the relation (
3.2.12
) (noting that convergence constraints (
3.2.10
) and (
3.2.11
) should be rewritten with
y\mapsto x_{i}
,
x\mapsto y_{j}^{-1}
), we find that

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{M}^{-1})\cdots\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{1}^{-1})\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle.

We conclude by noting that

\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{D}^{\bullet}(y_{j}^{-1})=\left\langle\varnothing\right|,

after which one has

\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{N,M}

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})}\left\langle\varnothing\right|\mathcal{C}(x_{1})\dots\mathcal{C}(x_{N})\left|2^{N},\varnothing\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})}F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

which is precisely the right hand side of (
3.4.10
).
∎

3.5.
Stable symmetric functions

Our goal in this section is to generalize the definition (
3.3.2
) of the rational symmetric functions
F_{S}
in a way that renders them stable; this generalization results in yet another family of functions denoted
H_{S}
. These functions are defined in Section
3.5.1
, and a direct limiting procedure that constructs them is outlined in Section
3.5.2
. Their basic properties, namely their symmetry and stability, are proved in Section
3.5.3
.

3.5.1.
Multivariate rational function
H_{S}

Before defining the rational function
H_{S}
, we shall require an extension of the previous inversion statistic (
2.5.1
) to
2
-strings:

Definition 3.5.1
.

Fix an integer
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and a vector
I=(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}
. We define the inversion number
{\rm inv}(I)
as follows:

(3.5.1)

\inv(I)=\sum_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant N}I_{i}(2-I_{j}).

Definition 3.5.2
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2K
. We introduce the rational function
H_{S}
as follows:

(3.5.2)

H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{I:|I|=2K}(-1)^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(I)/2}(1-q^{-1})^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(I)}q^{-\inv(I)}F_{S}^{I}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

with the sum taken over all vectors

I\in\{0,1,2\}^{N}
such that
|I|=2K
, and where

(3.5.3)

Remark 3.5.3
.

The functions (

. Indeed, taking

when

.

At the other extreme, when

, no particles may enter the lattice (

) and it freezes into a product of vertices

. We therefore have
H_{(0,0,0,\dots)}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=1
for any
N\geqslant 1
.

3.5.2.
Limiting procedure to obtain
H_{S}

The following theorem outlines how the functions
H_{S}
may be recovered via a suitable series of limits applied to the original family (
3.3.1
). The proof follows very similar lines to the corresponding result (Theorem (
2.5.4
)) in the six-vertex model: namely, we shall demonstrate certain simplified exchange relations for the row operators (
3.2.2
) that hold under the limits of the vertical spectral parameters that we impose.

Theorem 3.5.4
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
, and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2K
. Fix three alphabets
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
,
{\bm{u}}=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N-K})
and
{\bm{z}}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
of arbitrary parameters. The following relation then holds:

(3.5.4)

H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\frac{F_{(2^{N-K},S)}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})}{F_{(2^{N-K})}(*;\bm{u})},

where we write
\bm{u}\to\infty
as shorthand for the limits
u_{i}\rightarrow\infty
,
1\leqslant i\leqslant N-K
. The notation
(*;\bm{u})
indicates that the primary alphabet of
F_{(2^{N-K})}
may be chosen arbitrarily.

3.1

y\rightarrow\infty

only via their ratio, it is clear that all weights become independent of
x
after taking
y\rightarrow\infty
. We shall reflect this fact by suppressing the value of horizontal spectral parameters in most of the partition functions that follow.

.

Proof.

We begin with the proof of (
3.5.7
). Following very similar ideas to Proposition
3.2.4
, one may derive the following exchange relation between row-operators (of arbitrary length):

(3.5.9)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{2,a}(x;\bm{z})\mathcal{T}_{2,b}(y;\bm{z})=\sum_{c,d:c+d=a+b}W_{y/x}(d,c;b,a)\mathcal{T}_{2,d}(y;\bm{z})\mathcal{T}_{2,c}(x;\bm{z}),

where
a,b\in\{0,1,2\}
are arbitrary. After sending
\bm{z}\rightarrow\infty
, the row operators in (
3.5.9
) become independent of their primary arguments:

(3.5.10)

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{2,a}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{2,b}(*;\infty)=\sum_{c,d:c+d=a+b}W_{y/x}(d,c;b,a)\mathcal{T}_{2,d}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{2,c}(*;\infty),

which holds for arbitrary values of the parameter
y/x
. Consulting the weights in Figure
3.1
and sending
y/x\rightarrow\infty
, one finds that

\displaystyle W_{\infty}(d,c;b,a)=\bm{1}_{c=a}\cdot\bm{1}_{d=b}\cdot q^{-{\rm inv}(a,b)},\qquad\text{for}\ \ a>b,

and (
3.5.7
) then follows directly from (
3.5.10
).

The proof of (
3.5.8
) follows by similar reasoning. This time, one starts from (
3.5.10
) with
a=b=1
. Sending
y/x\rightarrow\infty
, there holds

\displaystyle W_{\infty}(d,c;1,1)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}0,&\quad c=0\ \text{and}\ d=2,\\
\\
-q^{-1},&\quad c=d=1,\\
\\
-q^{-4}(1-q)(1-q^{2}),&\quad c=2\ \text{and}\ d=0,\end{array}\right.

and (
3.5.10
) then reads

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(*;\infty)=-q^{-1}\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{2,1}(*;\infty)-q^{-4}(1-q)(1-q^{2})\mathcal{T}_{2,0}(*;\infty)\mathcal{T}_{2,2}(*;\infty).

This rearranges to yield (
3.5.8
).
∎

3.5.7
) and (
3.5.8
) is that the quantity

) and (

) proves (
3.5.6
), thereby completing the proof of Theorem
3.5.4
.

∎

3.5.3.
Symmetry and stability of
H_{S}

In this section, we discuss some properties of the rational functions defined by
(
3.5.2
)
. Similarly to their six-vertex analogues, the first property is that the rational functions
H_{S}
are symmetric with respect to their primary alphabet:

Proposition 3.5.6
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2K
. Then the rational function
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of Theorem
3.5.4
, in view of the fact that the right hand side of (
3.5.4
) is symmetric in
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.
∎

The second property is that the rational functions
(
3.5.2
)
are
stable
with respect to their alphabet

(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
:

Proposition 3.5.7
.

Fix two integers
K\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
,
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
such that
0\leqslant K\leqslant N
and let
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be a
2
-string such that
|S|=2K
. We then have the reduction property

\displaystyle H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1},x_{N}=\infty;\bm{z})=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\bm{z}),&\quad|S|\leqslant 2N-2,\\
\\
0,&\quad|S|=2N.\end{array}\right.

Proof.

Since
H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to its primary alphabet, we may equivalently study the limit as
x_{1}\rightarrow\infty
. This limit affects the bottommost row of vertices in the partition function (
3.5.3
). Consulting the table in Figure
3.1
, one finds that all weights
W_{z/x}(i,j;k,\ell)
have a well-defined limit as
x\rightarrow\infty
, and furthermore

(3.5.16)

\displaystyle\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}W_{z/x}(0,1;1,0)=0,\qquad\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}W_{z/x}(0,2;1,1)=0,\qquad\lim_{x\rightarrow\infty}W_{z/x}(0,2;2,0)=0.

It follows that
F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
vanishes if any of the vertices (
3.5.16
) occur within the first row of the partition function (
3.5.3
).

Let us begin by assuming that
|S|<2N
. The only way to prevent the appearance of one of the vertices (
3.5.16
) is to fix
I_{1}=0
, which causes the entire bottom row of the lattice to freeze away (since it is then comprised solely of
W_{0}(0,0;0,0)
vertices). As such, for any
I=(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})
we find that

\displaystyle F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\bm{1}_{I_{1}=0}\cdot F^{\tilde{I}}_{S}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),\qquad\tilde{I}=(I_{2},\dots,I_{N}),

which translates into the property

(3.5.17)

H_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\sum_{\tilde{I}:|\tilde{I}|=2K}(-1)^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(\tilde{I})/2}(1-q^{-1})^{\mathfrak{c}_{1}(\tilde{I})}q^{-\inv(\tilde{I})}F_{S}^{\tilde{I}}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\\
=H_{S}(x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

with the sum taken over vectors

\tilde{I}=(I_{2},\dots,I_{N})
, and where the first equality in (
3.5.17
) makes use of the fact that

\displaystyle\mathfrak{c}_{1}(0,I_{2},\dots,I_{N})

\displaystyle=\mathfrak{c}_{1}(I_{2},\dots,I_{N})=\mathfrak{c}_{1}(\tilde{I}),

\displaystyle\inv(0,I_{2},\dots,I_{N})

\displaystyle=\inv(I_{2},\dots,I_{N})=\inv(\tilde{I}).

This completes the proof of (
3.5.7
) in the case
|S|<2N
.

The case
|S|=2N
is handled very easily, since in this situation the vector that indexes the left incoming edges of the partition function (
3.5.3
) is forced, by conservation, to be
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})=(2^{N})
. As such, it is impossible to choose
I_{1}=0
, and
F^{I}_{S}(x_{1}=\infty,x_{2},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
vanishes identically.
∎

3.6.
Cauchy identity for stable symmetric functions

In Section
3.4
we stated a Cauchy-type identity between the rational symmetric functions (
3.3.1
) and (
3.3.4
). One aspect of the identity (
3.4.3
) which is somewhat undesirable is that its right hand side does not fully factorize. In this section we show that the stable symmetric functions (
3.5.2
) are more natural from this point of view, and satisfy a Cauchy summation identity with a fully factorized right hand side.

Theorem 3.6.1
.

Let
N,M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
be fixed positive integers. Fix parameters
q,x_{i},y_{j},z_{k}\in\mathbb{C}
such that for all
i\in\{1,\dots,N\}
,
j\in\{1,\dots,M\}
and
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the conditions (
3.4.1
) and (
3.4.2
) hold. We then have the summation identity

(3.6.1)

\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}(-1)^{|S|/2}q^{4MN-|S|^{2}}c_{S}(q)H_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})H_{S}(y_{1},\dots,y_{M};q^{-3}\bm{z}^{-1})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})},

where the constant
c_{S}(q)
is given by (
3.4.4
).

Proof.

Our starting point is the identity (
3.4.10
), in which we choose the secondary alphabet to be
\bm{u}\cup\bm{z}
, where
\bm{u}=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N})
and
\bm{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots)
:

\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})\\
=F_{(2^{N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})}.

Dividing this equation by
F_{(2^{N})}(*;\bm{u})
and taking the limit
\bm{u}\rightarrow\infty
, in exactly the same vein as (
3.5.4
), we read off the identity

(3.6.2)

\lim_{\bm{u}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{F_{(2^{N})}(*;\bm{u})}\cdot\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{M}\frac{(1-q^{2}x_{i}y_{j})(1-q^{3}x_{i}y_{j})}{(1-x_{i}y_{j})(1-qx_{i}y_{j})},

where the right hand side of (
3.6.2
) follows from (
3.5.4
) with
S=(0,0,0,\dots)
. It remains to show that the left hand side of (
3.6.2
) matches that of (
3.6.1
).

To that end, define the quantity

\displaystyle K_{N,M}:=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\sum_{S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)}F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,

\displaystyle x_{N};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z})G^{\bullet}_{S}(y_{1}^{-1},\dots,y_{M}^{-1};\bm{u}\cup\bm{z}),

which has the graphical representation

(3.6.3)

K_{N,M}=\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(I_{1},\dots,I_{N})\\

with
\chi
defined in (
3.5.11
), and where the factor of
q^{4MN}
arises from the above-mentioned normalization discrepancy between dotted and undotted vertices, while the
q
-inversions in the denominator of (
3.6.4
) are computed using the fact that

\displaystyle\inv(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})

\displaystyle=\inv(I_{1}\dots,I_{N})+\inv(J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})+|I||J|

\displaystyle=\inv(I_{1}\dots,I_{N})+\inv(J_{1},\dots,J_{M})+|I||J|.

By the invariance of
\chi
under re-partitioning of its arguments, we may choose
(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})=(0^{N},2^{M})
, which by (
3.5.12
) yields

\displaystyle\chi(I_{1},\dots,I_{N},J^{\bullet}_{M},\dots,J^{\bullet}_{1})=\chi(0^{N},2^{M})=\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}F_{(2^{N})}(*;\bm{u}).

We have thus derived the equation

(3.6.5)

\lim_{\bm{u}\to\infty}\frac{K_{N,M}}{F_{(2^{N})}(*;\bm{u})}=\\

3.7.
Properties of rational symmetric functions

This section serves as a prelude to the next one. Our aim is to provide a list of properties satisfied by the rational symmetric functions
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
, before writing down a solution to these properties in Section
3.8
.

In Section
3.7.1
, we state a family of exchange relations obeyed by the function
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
. These relations allow one to start from an arbitrary
2
-string
S
and progressively order it. More precisely, these relations provide a way to convert an arbitrary function
F_{S}
into a linear combination of functions
F_{T}
, such that each
T\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
in this sum has the form
T_{1}\geqslant T_{2}\geqslant T_{3}\geqslant\cdots
. We shall refer to such
2
-strings as
ordered
.

In Section
3.7.2
, we use the lattice formulation of
F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
to derive recursion relations that it satisfies when the indexing
2
-string
T
is ordered. These recursion relations provide the foundation for standard Lagrange interpolation techniques.

Finally, in Section
3.7.3
, we prove that all of these properties are uniquely-determining, meaning that any family of functions that obey the properties must be equal to
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
itself.

3.7.1.
Exchange relations

Definition 3.7.1
.

Fix an integer
k\geqslant 1
and let
S,T\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
be
2
-strings such that
(S_{k},S_{k+1})\not=(T_{k},T_{k+1})
, but
S_{k}+S_{k+1}=T_{k}+T_{k+1}
, and
S_{i}=T_{i}
for all
i\not=k,k+1
. We say that
S,T
are
k
-exchangeable and write
S\sim_{k}T
.

Proposition 3.7.2
.

Fix an integer
k\geqslant 1
and a
2
-string
S\in\mathfrak{s}(2)
such that
S_{k}<S_{k+1}
. The following relation then holds:

(3.7.1)

W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(S_{k+1},S_{k};S_{k+1},S_{k})F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\\
F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})-\sum_{T:S\sim_{k}T}W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(T_{k+1},T_{k};S_{k+1},S_{k})F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}),

with the sum taken over
2
-strings
T
such that
S,T
are
k
-exchangeable, and where
\sigma_{k}\cdot S=(\dots,S_{k+1},S_{k},\dots)
,
\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z}=(\dots,z_{k+1},z_{k},\dots)
denote transposition of the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th elements of
S,\bm{z}
.

Proof.

The proof is by application of the Yang–Baxter equation (
3.1.8
) to the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th columns of the partition function in question.

In particular, starting from the lattice representation of
F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})
, one may attach a frozen
W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(0,0;0,0)
vertex at the base of the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th columns. By repeated application of the Yang–Baxter equation, this vertex emerges from the top of the same columns, leading to the identity

where the states assigned to external horizontal edges are arbitrary, but held fixed on both sides of the equation. We then read off the equation

\displaystyle F_{\sigma_{k}\cdot S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{k}\cdot\bm{z})=\sum_{T}W_{z_{k+1}/z_{k}}(T_{k+1},T_{k};S_{k+1},S_{k})F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})

where the sum is over
2
-strings such that
T_{i}=S_{i}
for all
i\not=k,k+1
. Equation (
3.7.1
) then follows by rearrangement.
∎

Remark 3.7.3
.

While the
k
-th and
(k+1)
-th elements of
S
in Proposition
3.7.2
are increasing, it is easily seen that all
2
-strings present on the right hand side of (
3.7.1
) are non-increasing with respect to the same two elements. It is therefore possible to iterate (
3.7.1
), converting an arbitrary initial
2
-string into a linear combination of non-increasing ones.

Proposition 3.7.4
.

Fix an integer
N\geqslant 1
. The following relation holds:

(3.7.2)

W_{z_{2}/z_{1}}(1,1;2,0)F_{(1^{2N})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\\
F_{(2,0,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{1}\cdot\bm{z})-W_{z_{2}/z_{1}}(0,2;2,0)F_{(2,0,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\\
-W_{z_{2}/z_{1}}(2,0;2,0)\prod_{i=1}^{N}W_{z_{1}/x_{i}}(0,2;0,2)F_{(2,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),

where
\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}=(z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
denotes the secondary alphabet with the omission of
z_{1}
.

Proof.

The proof follows along similar lines to that of Proposition
3.7.2
. This time, one starts from the lattice representation of
F_{(2,0,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{1}\cdot\bm{z})
and attaches a frozen
W_{z_{2}/z_{1}}(0,0;0,0)
vertex at the base of the first and second columns. By repeated application of the Yang–Baxter equation, this vertex emerges from the top of the same columns, leading to the identity

where the states assigned to left horizontal edges are all
2
, as that coincides with the left boundary of the partition function (
3.3.2
). We then obtain the equation

(3.7.3)

\displaystyle F_{(2,0,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\sigma_{1}\cdot\bm{z})=\sum_{(a,b):a+b=2}W_{z_{2}/z_{1}}(b,a;2,0)F_{(a,b,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

The sum over
(a,b)
such that
a+b=2
consists of three possible pairs: namely,
(a,b)=(2,0)
,
(a,b)=(1,1)
and
(a,b)=(0,2)
. The final of these leads to a simplification of the function
F_{(a,b,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
:

(3.7.4)

\displaystyle F_{(0,2,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}W_{z_{1}/x_{i}}(0,2;0,2)F_{(2,1^{2N-2})}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),

which is easily deduced by freezing of the first column of the partition function (
3.3.2
) for
F_{S}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
when
S_{1}=0
. Combining (
3.7.3
) and (
3.7.4
) then yields the result (
3.7.2
).
∎

Remark 3.7.5
.

Collectively, Propositions
3.7.2
and
3.7.4
have the following implication: not only is it possible to completely order the
2
-strings that index our symmetric functions, it is also possible to ensure that every ordered
2
-string begins with a
2
.

To see this, recall that Proposition
3.7.2
allows
F_{S}
to be written as a linear combination of functions
F_{T}
, where
T
is ordered. If
T=(1^{2N})
, the only ordered
2
-string that does not begin with
2
, application of Proposition
3.7.4
results in a linear combination of
2
-strings that begin with
2
. While not all of the
2
-strings appearing on the right hand side of (
3.7.2
) are non-increasing, renewed application of (
3.7.1
) allows the strings
(2,0,1^{2N-2})
to be ordered (without disturbing the
2
at the head of the string).

3.7.2.
Recursion relations

Proposition 3.7.6
.

Fix integers
N\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and
M\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}
such that
N>M
, and let
T=(2^{N-M},1^{2M})
denote a non-increasing
2
-string. The function
F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
satisfies the following properties:

(1)

The function
F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})
is symmetric with respect to its primary alphabet
(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
.

(2)

Introduce the normalized function

\tilde{F}_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\prod_{j=1}^{N+M}(x_{i}-q^{2}z_{j})(x_{i}-q^{3}z_{j})F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z}).

Then
\tilde{F}_{T}
is a polynomial in
z_{1}
of degree
2N
.

(3)

The function
F_{T}
vanishes at
z_{1}=0
:

\displaystyle F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=0}=0.

(4)

The function
F_{T}
has the following recursion relation with respect to
z_{1}
:

\displaystyle F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big|_{z_{1}=x_{N}}=F_{T\backslash 2}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),

where
\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}=(z_{2},z_{3},\dots)
denotes the secondary alphabet with the omission of
z_{1}
and
T\backslash 2=(2^{N-M-1},1^{2M})
.

(5)

The function
F_{T}
has a further recursion relation with respect to
z_{1}
:

(3.7.5)

{\rm Res}\Big\{F_{T}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N};\bm{z})\Big\}_{z_{1}=q^{-3}x_{N}}=-\frac{(1-q^{2})(1-q^{3})}{q^{6}(1-q)}x_{N}\\[5.0pt]
\times\prod_{i=1}^{N-1}\frac{(x_{N}-q^{2}x_{i})(x_{N}-q^{3}x_{i})}{(x_{N}-x_{i})(x_{N}-qx_{i})}\prod_{j=2}^{N+M}\frac{(x_{N}-z_{j})(x_{N}-qz_{j})}{(x_{N}-q^{2}z_{j})(x_{N}-q^{3}z_{j})}\sum_{U}\Phi_{U}F_{U}(x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1};\widehat{\bm{z}}_{1}),

with the sum taken over
2
-strings
U=(U_{2},\dots,U_{N+M})
such that
|U|=2N-2
, and where the coefficients
\Phi_{U}
are defined as the one-row partition functions

(3.7.6)

\Phi_{U}\equiv\Phi_{(U_{2},\dots,U_{N+M})}=\raisebox{-68.2866pt}{
